a: Setting the heart's thoughts in order
t: Plans set out like a battle line
p: The word for plans is the one used for setting troops in line or laying out wood on the altar.
b: Ma'arkhe lev, "the arrangements of the heart", uses a word for setting things in rows: soldiers drawn up for battle (1 Samuel 17:8), wood laid on the altar (Genesis 22:9), bread set out in the sanctuary. A person can lay out his thoughts that carefully, the saying grants, but the "answer of the tongue", what actually comes out when the moment arrives, is the LORD's. Readers have taken this two ways. Many (Rashi, most modern commentators) read it as God's rule over the outcome of human plans, like 16:9 and 19:21. Others see a sharper point about speech: you can rehearse, but you cannot control the words you finally say. Jesus' promise that the Spirit will give his followers words before courts has often been read beside this verse (Matthew 10:19–20).
orig: מַעַרְכֵי־לֵב (ma'arkhe-lev), 'arrangements of the heart'; מַעֲנֵה לָשׁוֹן (ma'aneh lashon), 'answer of the tongue'

a: the LORD is the one who weighs spirits
p: In Egyptian belief the dead person's heart was weighed on scales at judgment. Proverbs gives the scales to the LORD.
b: The verb tokhen means to measure or weigh. Proverbs uses it three times of God, who "weighs spirits" here and "weighs hearts" in 21:2 and 24:12. Egyptian readers knew a famous scene: in the Book of the Dead the heart of the dead person is set on a balance against the feather of Maat, the goddess of truth and order, while the god Thoth records the result. The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, which Proverbs echoes later (see 22:17), gives a whole chapter to honest balances and the god who guards them (Amenemope chapter 16). Many scholars think Proverbs borrows the image and turns it: there is no judgment hall of many gods, only the LORD, and he does the weighing now, in this life, not only after death. Whether a direct borrowing or a shared figure of speech, the point is that a person's own verdict on himself is not the one that counts (1 Samuel 16:7; 1 Corinthians 4:4).
orig: וְתֹכֵן רוּחוֹת יְהוָה (vetokhen ruchot YHWH), 'and the LORD weighs spirits'

a: Roll what you do onto the LORD
p: The Hebrew verb is 'roll', as you roll a heavy stone or a load off your back.
b: Most English Bibles say "commit". The Hebrew gol is the command form of galal, "to roll", used for rolling a stone from a well (Genesis 29:3, 8, 10) or away from a cave (Joshua 10:18). The picture is of a load too heavy to carry, rolled over onto someone stronger. Psalm 37:5 uses the same image ("roll your way onto the LORD"), and Psalm 22:8 has the mockers sneer at a man who "rolled" his cause onto the LORD. The promise is not that every plan will succeed. It is that plans handed over to God become firm (kun, the same verb as "fixes" in 16:9). The Greek has no form of this verse: it lacks 16:1 and 16:3, places 16:6–8 at the end of its chapter 15, and opens its chapter 16 with a form of 16:9.
orig: גֹּל אֶל־יְהוָה (gol el-YHWH), 'roll to the LORD'

a: with its purpose in view
t: For its purpose, or for himself?
p: The Hebrew can mean 'for its answer' (its fitting end) or 'for himself'. The line on the wicked troubles readers.
b: Lamma'anehu is unusual. Most modern scholars take it as "for its answer", that is, for its fitting purpose or counterpart: everything in God's world has its matching outcome, and the wicked have theirs in the day of disaster. The KJV, following the Latin (propter semet ipsum), has "for himself", and some readers took this to mean that God created certain people in order to destroy them. Rashi reads "for his praise". The proverb's own concern is narrower than later debates about predestination: wickedness does not escape God's order, and the evil day the wicked bring on others becomes their own (compare 16:5; Romans 9:22 is often cited beside it). The Greek gives a gentler version: "All the works of the Lord are done with righteousness, and the ungodly man is kept for the evil day" (the Greek 16:9).
orig: לַמַּעֲנֵהוּ (lamma'anehu), 'for its answer / its purpose'

a: you can shake hands on it
p: Literally 'hand to hand': a handshake that seals a deal. Here it means 'you can be sure of it'.
b: The Hebrew says only "hand to hand". The same phrase opens 11:21 ("You can shake hands on it: the evil man will not go free"), and this site renders both alike. The picture is two people striking hands to seal an agreement, the same gesture as the pledge in 17:18 and 22:26. Older readers took it differently: the KJV, "though hand join in hand", means that even proud people who band together will not escape. The modern reading, "be assured", fits both verses better. "Abhorrent" renders to'evah, something the LORD finds disgusting, a word Proverbs uses for moral wrongs such as pride, lies and dishonest scales (16:12; 17:15; 20:10, 23).
orig: יָד לְיָד (yad leyad), 'hand to hand'; תּוֹעֲבַת יְהוָה (to'avat YHWH), 'abhorrent to the LORD'

a: Guilt is atoned for by loyal love and faithfulness
p: Proverbs says guilt is 'atoned for' by loyal love and faithfulness. Jews and Christians have read this very differently.
b: The verb is kipper, the word for atonement in the sacrifices (Leviticus 4:20; 16:30). Proverbs does not mention sacrifice. Whose loyal love and faithfulness? It may be God's, as often when hesed and 'emet are paired (Exodus 34:6; Psalm 85:10): he covers guilt by his own faithfulness. Or it may be the person's, as in 3:3 and 20:28: a life of loyal love sets right what wrongdoing broke. The Greek took the second way and wrote "By almsgiving and acts of faithfulness sins are purged away" (the Greek 15:27a; compare Daniel 4:27; Tobit 12:9; Sirach 3:30). The Talmud cites this verse to show that Torah study and kind deeds atone for sin (Berakhot 5a–b, where chesed is read as acts of kindness, with 21:21, and emet as Torah, with 23:23). After the Temple fell, Jewish teaching put deeds of loyal love in the place of sacrifice. Christians differ on what this means for forgiveness; see the card on the chapter page.
r: 3:3–4; 20:28; 10:12; Exodus 34:6; Leviticus 16:30; Daniel 4:27; Tobit 12:9; Sirach 3:30; 1 Peter 4:8

a: the LORD fixes where his steps fall
p: One of the Bible's best-known sayings on plans and providence. Egypt's Amenemope says something similar.
b: The heart "maps out" (yechashev, thinks, calculates) a road, but the LORD "fixes" (yakhin, makes firm, sets) the steps. The saying belongs to a group in this collection (16:1, 9, 33; 19:21; 20:24; 21:30–31) that set human planning inside God's rule without making planning pointless: Proverbs urges careful plans in the same breath (20:18; 21:5). The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope has a close thought: the words people say are one thing, and what the god does is another (Amenemope chapter 18, as translated by Lichtheim). Jeremiah prays that a person's way is not in his own power (Jeremiah 10:23), and James warns traders who say "tomorrow we will go" to add "if the Lord wills" (James 4:13–15). The Latin proverb "man proposes, God disposes" (Thomas à Kempis) is a later echo.
orig: וַיהוָה יָכִין צַעֲדוֹ (vaYHWH yakhin tsa'ado), 'but the LORD makes firm his step'

a: There is divination on a king's lips
p: The word is qesem, 'divination', a practice the Law forbids. Here it means the king speaks with an oracle's authority.
b: Qesem is the word for the fortune-telling the Law bans (Deuteronomy 18:10) and that Saul is condemned for (1 Samuel 15:23). Using it of Israel's king is startling. The point is that a king's verdict has the force of an oracle, a decision from above, as when the woman of Tekoa tells David that he is "like God's angel" in hearing out good and evil (2 Samuel 14:17, 20) or when Solomon judges between the two mothers (1 Kings 3:28). The second line can be a statement ("in judgment his mouth does not act unfaithfully") or, as in the Plain, a duty ("must not"). Read the first way, the verse is court flattery. Read the second, it is a charge: the king's words carry so much weight that they must never be unfaithful. Rashi applies it to any wise man who sits as judge.
orig: קֶסֶם עַל־שִׂפְתֵי־מֶלֶךְ (qesem 'al-sifte-melekh), 'divination on the lips of a king'

a: every stone in the bag of weights
p: Merchants carried stone weights in a bag. Many have been found, marked with their value.
b: Before coins, silver was weighed on a hand balance against stone weights carried in a pouch. Archaeologists have found many such weights in Judah, small polished limestone domes marked with a sign and a number, usually in multiples of the shekel (about 11.4 grams). Their actual weights vary somewhat even when the marks are the same, which shows how easily a dishonest trader could keep a light set for selling and a heavy one for buying. The Law forbids exactly that (Deuteronomy 25:13–15; Leviticus 19:35–36), and Proverbs returns to it three times (11:1; 20:10, 23). Here the saying goes further: the whole system of honest measure is the LORD's own work, so cheating on a weight is an offense against him, not only against the buyer.

a: Kings find it abhorrent to act wickedly
p: The Hebrew can mean that kings hate wickedness, or that wickedness done by kings is abhorrent.
b: To'avat melakhim 'asot resha' is literally "an abhorrence of kings is doing wickedness". The Plain takes kings as the ones who abhor it: a good king hates wrongdoing, since righteousness holds up his throne. The words can also mean that wickedness done by kings is abhorrent, to the LORD and to their people, and so a warning to kings. In 16:13 the Hebrew has plural "kings" with a singular verb ("he loves"); the Plain makes it singular, "a king", since the saying describes any king. Both verses picture the ideal, not every king (compare 28:15–16; 29:12).
orig: תּוֹעֲבַת מְלָכִים עֲשׂוֹת רֶשַׁע (to'avat melakhim 'asot resha')

a: death's messengers
p: At an ancient court the king's anger could mean execution. A wise courtier knew how to calm it.
b: "Messengers of death" pictures the officers sent out to carry out a death sentence, as Solomon sent Benaiah against Adonijah, Joab and Shimei (1 Kings 2:25, 29–34, 46). Sayings 16:10–15 form a small group about the king, with a matching pair of opposites: his fury is death (16:14), the light of his face is life (16:15). The wise man "calms" it, literally "covers" or "atones for" it (kipper), the same verb as in 16:6: he finds the words or the gift that turn the king's anger away, as Abigail did with David (1 Samuel 25:23–35). These sayings show that at least part of this collection was shaped for young men who would serve at court (see the chapter page). The Talmud applied the verse to visiting a sage to pray for a sick person (Bava Batra 116a).
orig: מַלְאֲכֵי־מָוֶת (mal'akhe-mavet), 'messengers of death'; יְכַפְּרֶנָּה (yekhapperennah), 'will cover/atone for it'

a: a cloud heavy with the late rains
p: The malqosh rains of March and April filled out the grain before harvest. A king's favor was that welcome.
b: Israel's rains came in two seasons that framed the growing year: the early rains in October and November softened the ground for plowing, and the late rains (malqosh) in March and April swelled the grain just before harvest (Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 5:24; Joel 2:23). A cloud bringing the late rain meant a full harvest after months of waiting. The image is of a king's goodwill as a life-giving gift that comes from above, which no subject can command. The shining face echoes the priestly blessing, where the LORD makes his face shine on his people (Numbers 6:25), and many psalms ask the same of God (Psalm 4:6; Psalm 80:3).
orig: כְּעָב מַלְקוֹשׁ (ke'av malqosh), 'like a cloud of the late rain'
r: Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 5:24; Joel 2:23; Job 29:23; Numbers 6:25; Psalm 4:6; 19:12

a: Pride comes before a crash
p: Commonly quoted as 'pride goes before a fall'. The Hebrew has two different pictures: a breaking, and a stumble.
b: The popular saying blends the two lines. The first line says pride (ga'on) comes before shever, a breaking or crash, the word used for a shattered pot or a broken city. The second says a lofty spirit, literally "height of spirit", comes before kishalon, a stumbling. The pairing is a little joke: the higher you hold your head, the less you see the stone in the road. The same thought returns in 18:12 and 29:23, and in the New Testament James and Peter quote the Greek of 3:34, that God opposes the proud (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). Ancient Greek readers knew the idea as hubris followed by ruin; the Greek translator in fact uses hubris here.
orig: לִפְנֵי־שֶׁבֶר גָּאוֹן (lifne-shever ga'on), 'before a breaking, pride'; כִּשָּׁלוֹן (kishalon), 'stumbling'

a: Pay attention to the word
p: The Hebrew davar can mean a word, a matter or business. Readers disagree whether it is God's word or practical affairs.
b: Maskil 'al davar can mean "one who pays attention to the word" or "one who handles a matter with skill" (so the KJV, "he that handleth a matter wisely"). Since the second line speaks of trusting the LORD, many readers, Jewish and Christian, take "the word" as teaching, whether the sage's or God's (compare 13:13, where "a word" stands beside "a command"). Others see a contrast between practical skill and faith, or a pairing: skill in affairs and trust in God together bring good. The Plain keeps the wording open. "How happy" renders 'ashre, the word that opens Psalm 1.
orig: מַשְׂכִּיל עַל־דָּבָר (maskil 'al-davar), 'one who gives attention to a word/matter'

a: the discipline of stubborn fools is folly
p: Either the 'teaching' fools give is folly, or folly itself is the fool's punishment.
b: Musar covers both teaching and punishment (see the note at 1:2). So the line can mean that the instruction fools give is worthless, or that their folly is itself their punishment: they are disciplined by the results of their own foolishness. Many modern commentators prefer the second, since it gives a neat contrast with the first line: good sense is a spring that feeds its owner, folly is a whip that beats its owner. The word for these fools is 'evil, the "stubborn fool" who will not be taught (see the note at 1:7).
orig: מוּסַר אֱוִלִים אִוֶּלֶת (musar 'evilim 'ivvelet), 'the discipline of stubborn fools is folly'

a: There is a road that looks straight to a person
p: This saying is word for word the same as 14:12, and the Plain renders both alike.
b: The Hebrew of 16:25 repeats 14:12 exactly. Proverbs contains many such doublets, and they are one sign that the book was put together from collections that overlapped (see the chapter page). Here the repeat may also be placed on purpose: it closes a run of sayings about the heart and the tongue, and stands just before the sayings on the laborer and the troublemaker. The "roads of death" are plural, as if the one straight-looking road branched into many ways to die. Christians have often read the verse beside Jesus' saying about the wide road that leads to destruction (Matthew 7:13–14).

a: A laborer's appetite labors on his behalf
p: The Hebrew plays on one root: the toiler's appetite toils for him. Hunger is a hard boss, but it gets work done.
b: Nefesh 'amel 'amelah lo: the root 'amal, toil, appears twice, and the Plain keeps the echo ("laborer ... labors"). Nefesh here is the appetite, the throat and its hunger (as in Isaiah 5:14). The second line has a rare verb, akaf, probably "press" or "urge", as a driver urges a load-animal. The saying is neither praise nor blame: it observes that need is what keeps most people working (compare Ecclesiastes 6:7). The rabbis applied it to Torah study: a student must work at learning with his mouth, by constant review (Sanhedrin 99b).
orig: נֶפֶשׁ עָמֵל עָמְלָה לּוֹ (nefesh 'amel 'amelah lo)

a: A worthless man
p: Beliyya'al means 'worthless', a man of no value. Later Jewish writings turned it into a name for Satan.
b: "A man of beliyya'al" is a scoundrel or troublemaker (6:12; 1 Samuel 25:25; 1 Kings 21:10); this site renders the word "worthless" throughout. Its origin is debated (perhaps "without worth" or "of no rising"). In the Dead Sea Scrolls Belial becomes the name of the leader of the forces of darkness, and Paul uses the name for Satan (2 Corinthians 6:15). Here it is still a human type: a man who "digs up" evil, either digging a pit for others (26:27) or digging up scandal to spread. His speech "burns like fire", an image James develops (James 3:6). The next three verses describe his kind: the twisted man, the gossip and the violent man.
orig: אִישׁ בְּלִיַּעַל (ish beliyya'al), 'a man of worthlessness'

a: a gossip
p: Nirgan, 'whisperer' or 'gossip', appears only in Proverbs: here, in 18:8, and twice in 26.
b: Nirgan comes from a root meaning to grumble or murmur (Deuteronomy 1:27; Psalm 106:25). In Proverbs it is the person who passes along damaging talk in low tones, a "whisperer" (16:28; 18:8; 26:20, 22). It is a different word from rakhil, the "talebearer" who "goes around" spreading what he hears (11:13; 20:19). The gossip's target here is the 'alluf, the close friend or trusted companion (the word can also mean a chief). Gossip does its worst damage to the closest bonds, because only close friends have secrets to betray. Compare 17:9, where bringing a matter up again does the same.
orig: נִרְגָּן (nirgan), 'whisperer, gossip'; אַלּוּף ('alluf), 'close friend'

a: He shuts his eyes to plot twisted things
p: Shutting the eyes and pressing the lips were gestures of a man plotting. Proverbs often reads the body.
b: Proverbs pays close attention to gestures: the winking eye (6:13; 10:10), the pointing finger, the shuffling feet (6:13). Here the plotter "shuts" his eyes (a rare verb, 'otseh), perhaps narrowing them in calculation, and "presses" his lips (qorets, the verb used for winking in 10:10), a tight-mouthed sign that the plan is set. The second line is almost a stage direction: the lips close, and the harm is as good as done. Such sayings trained young officials to read people at court before they acted.
orig: עֹצֶה עֵינָיו ('otseh 'enav), 'shutting his eyes'; קֹרֵץ שְׂפָתָיו (qorets sefatav), 'pressing his lips'

a: Gray hair is a crown of beauty
t: Gray hair and the righteous life
p: Old age is pictured as a reward of righteousness. Proverbs states the rule; Job and Ecclesiastes test it.
b: Long life is one of wisdom's promised gifts (3:2, 16; 9:11; 10:27), and gray hair is its visible sign (20:29). Leviticus commands Israelites to rise before the gray-headed (Leviticus 19:32). Read as a promise, the saying would be contradicted by the many righteous people who die young, a problem Job and Ecclesiastes press hard (Job 21:7; Ecclesiastes 7:15). Most interpreters read it as Proverbs' sayings are generally meant: a statement of how life usually goes in a world God orders, not a guarantee for each case. Others read the second line as a condition: gray hair is a crown only when it is found on the way of righteousness, so an old fool earns no honor (compare Sirach 25:4–6).

a: ruling your own spirit beats capturing a town
p: Self-control is greater than conquest. The rabbis built a famous saying on this verse.
b: "Slow to anger" is literally "long of nostrils", the same phrase used of God in Exodus 34:6. The second line contrasts "ruling" (moshel) one's own spirit with capturing a city, the greatest feat of an ancient soldier. The Mishnah answers the question "Who is mighty?" with "The one who subdues his impulse," quoting this verse (Mishnah Avot 4:1). Greek moralists said much the same about self-mastery. Proverbs links it to its many sayings on anger and patience (14:29; 15:18; 19:11; 25:28, where a man without self-control is a city with its walls broken down).
orig: אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם ('erekh appayim), 'long of nostrils, slow to anger'

a: People throw the lot into the lap
p: Lots were thrown from the fold of a garment. Israel used them to divide land and choose people, leaving the result to God.
b: The lot (goral) was probably a set of marked stones or sticks shaken in the fold of a robe (the "lap", cheq) and thrown out. Israel used lots to divide the land among the tribes (Joshua 18:6–10), to choose the goat for the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:8), to find a guilty party (Joshua 7:14–18; Jonah 1:7) and to assign priestly duties (1 Chronicles 24:5). The Urim and Thummim may have worked in a similar way. The saying does not tell readers to make decisions by lot; it says that even the most random-seeming outcome is the LORD's "verdict" (mishpat). 18:18 adds that the lot can end quarrels. The apostles' last use of the lot, choosing Matthias, comes before Pentecost (Acts 1:26).
orig: בַּחֵיק יוּטַל אֶת־הַגּוֹרָל (bacheq yutal et-haggoral), 'into the lap the lot is thrown'
r: 18:18; Joshua 18:6–10; Leviticus 16:8; Joshua 7:14–18; Jonah 1:7; 1 Chronicles 24:5; Acts 1:26; Esther 3:7

a: sacrificial feasts
p: The Hebrew says 'sacrifices of strife'. Meat was rare, and a family ate it mostly at sacrificial meals.
b: Ordinary Israelites seldom ate meat. When they did, it was usually at a sacrifice: in a peace offering the fat and blood went to God and most of the meat was eaten by the worshiper's household and guests (Leviticus 7:11–18; 1 Samuel 1:4–5; 1 Samuel 20:6). So a "house full of sacrifices" is a house full of feasting, and the saying sets it against a dry crust. The irony is pointed: a meal that should mark peace with God and neighbor (shelamim, "peace offerings") is spoiled by quarreling. The "better than" saying is a favorite form in this collection (15:16–17; 16:8, 19, 32; 19:1, 22; 21:9, 19); Amenemope has its own versions (see 15:17 and 22:17).
orig: זִבְחֵי־רִיב (zivche-riv), 'sacrifices of strife'

a: A servant with good sense
p: In Israel a capable slave could rise high, even marry into the family and share the inheritance.
b: 'Eved means a servant or slave; this site renders it by context. Here it is a household slave who "acts with good sense" (maskil), set against a son who "brings disgrace" (mevish, the shameful son of 10:5). Such reversals happened. Abraham, before Isaac's birth, expected his servant Eliezer to be his heir (Genesis 15:2–3); Sheshan gave his daughter to his Egyptian slave Jarha (1 Chronicles 2:34–35); Ziba managed Saul's estate (2 Samuel 9:9–10). Ancient Mesopotamian contracts also record slaves adopted as heirs. The saying warns a privileged son that birth alone will not keep his place. Compare 30:22, where a slave who becomes king is one of the things the earth cannot bear, and 19:10.
orig: עֶבֶד־מַשְׂכִּיל ('eved-maskil), 'a servant who acts wisely'

a: Silver goes in the melting pot and gold in the furnace
p: Metal was heated to separate it from waste. The LORD tests hearts the same way.
b: The matsref is a crucible for melting silver, and the kur a smelting furnace. Refining heated the ore until the dross could be skimmed off, leaving pure metal. The Bible often uses the picture for testing that purifies (Psalm 66:10; Isaiah 48:10; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:2–3). The verb bochen, "tests", is used of God examining hearts in Psalm 7:9 and Jeremiah 17:10. The first line comes back word for word in 27:21, where the test is praise. Peter applies the image to faith tested by trials, more precious than gold refined by fire (1 Peter 1:7).
orig: מַצְרֵף לַכֶּסֶף וְכוּר לַזָּהָב (matsref lakkesef vekhur lazzahav)
r: 27:21; Psalm 66:10; Isaiah 48:10; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:2–3; Jeremiah 17:10; 1 Peter 1:7

a: Mocking a poor man is taunting the one who made him
p: The first line nearly repeats 14:31. Whoever mocks the poor insults God, who made the poor man.
b: The verb here is lo'eg, "mock", where 14:31 has 'osheq, "oppress"; the rest of the line is the same, and the Plain keeps the wording of 14:31. The thought is that every person is God's work, so contempt for the poor reaches past the poor man to his Maker (22:2; Job 31:15). The second line moves from contempt to glee: enjoying someone else's disaster. Job swears he never rejoiced at his enemy's ruin (Job 31:29), and Obadiah condemns Edom for gloating over Jerusalem (Obadiah 12). The Greek adds a third line: "but the one who has compassion will receive mercy", which recalls Matthew 5:7. The Talmud applies the verse to failing to escort the dead to burial (Berakhot 18a).

a: children find their glory in their fathers
p: The Hebrew avot is 'fathers'. It can include both parents and earlier ancestors.
b: Avotam is "their fathers", the usual word for fathers or ancestors. In Hebrew, as in many languages, the masculine plural can include mothers too, and some modern versions render "parents". The Plain keeps "fathers" because the first line also looks back up the generations: grandchildren are the crown of the old, and children take pride in the line they come from. In a society where a person was known as "son of" someone, a good father's name was a real inheritance (compare 22:1). The Greek adds a saying here: "The faithful man has the whole world of wealth, but the faithless not even a penny" (the Greek 17:6a).
orig: וְתִפְאֶרֶת בָּנִים אֲבוֹתָם (vetif'eret banim avotam), 'and the glory of children is their fathers'

a: Lofty words are out of place for a godless fool
t: Fine words and the godless fool
p: Nabal is the 'godless fool', the boor with no regard for God or decency, like Nabal the husband of Abigail.
b: Nabal is a fool of a different kind from the kesil or the 'evil: a person without shame, coarse and hard toward God and people (Psalm 14:1; Isaiah 32:5–6). The best-known example is Nabal, Abigail's husband, of whom she says, "Nabal is his name, and shameful folly is his companion" (1 Samuel 25:25). Sefat yeter, "a lip of excess", may mean lofty, eloquent speech or arrogant speech; either way it does not fit him. The second line argues "how much less": if fine words are wrong in a boor's mouth, lies are far worse in a noble's (nadiv, a person of rank or a generous person). Rank brings a duty to tell the truth.
orig: שְׂפַת־יֶתֶר (sefat-yeter), 'a lip of excess'; נָבָל (nabal), 'godless fool'

a: A bribe is a magic stone in the eyes of its owner
p: Proverbs describes how bribes work (17:8; 18:16; 21:14) and also condemns them (17:23). Readers weigh the two.
b: The Hebrew says a bribe is 'even chen, "a stone of favor", probably a lucky charm or amulet that brings success, and only "in the eyes of its owner", that is, in the giver's opinion. Several sayings observe that gifts open doors and calm anger (18:16; 19:6; 21:14). Yet 17:23 condemns the wicked who take bribes to bend justice, and the Law forbids judges to accept them (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19). Most commentators conclude that Proverbs sometimes simply reports how the world works, leaving the reader to judge. Some distinguish an honest gift (mattan, 18:16) from a corrupting bribe (shochad, here and 17:23). Rashi turned it into praise of repentance as a jewel before God.
orig: אֶבֶן־חֵן הַשֹּׁחַד ('even-chen hashshochad), 'a stone of favor is the bribe'

a: Laying a cover over a wrong is how you go after love
p: Covering an offense, not repeating it, keeps friendship. 10:12 says love covers all wrongdoing; 1 Peter 4:8 echoes it.
b: To "cover" (mekhasseh) a wrong here is not to hide a crime from justice (28:13 condemns covering one's own sins) but to refuse to keep bringing up a friend's offense. 10:12 says the same: "love lays a cover over all wrongdoing", a line that 1 Peter 4:8 and James 5:20 echo. The second line is the opposite: the one who "repeats a matter" (shoneh vedavar), going back over it again and again, or retelling it to others, "splits up close friends", the same phrase as the gossip's work in 16:28.

a: a merciless messenger will be sent against him
p: A royal officer, an angel of punishment, or disaster itself. The Greek says 'the Lord will send'.
b: The rebel (meri, rebellion) may be rebelling against the king or against God. The "cruel messenger" may be a royal officer sent to arrest or kill him (compare 16:14, "death's messengers"), or an angel of judgment like the destroying angels of Psalm 78:49. The Greek makes God the sender: "the Lord will send out a merciless angel against him." The verse is a warning to anyone at court tempted to plot, as Absalom or Sheba did (2 Samuel 15:10–12; 2 Samuel 20:1–2, 21–22).
orig: וּמַלְאָךְ אַכְזָרִי יְשֻׁלַּח־בּוֹ (umal'akh akhzari yeshullach-bo)

a: a mother bear robbed of her cubs
t: The bear robbed of her cubs
p: Bears lived in Israel's hills. A mother who had lost her cubs was the most dangerous animal a traveler could meet.
b: The Syrian brown bear lived in Israel's wooded hills into the last century. A she-bear robbed of her cubs (dov shakkul) was proverbial for fury: Hushai compares David's men to one (2 Samuel 17:8), and the LORD compares himself to one in judgment (Hosea 13:8). Two she-bears mauled the boys who mocked Elisha (2 Kings 2:24). The saying claims that a fool in the middle of his folly is worse: the bear's anger has a cause and an end, but the fool's folly has neither.
orig: פָּגוֹשׁ דֹּב שַׁכּוּל (pagosh dov shakkul), 'let a bereaved bear meet'

a: Whoever repays good with evil
p: David is the classic case: Nathan told him the sword would not leave his house.
b: Repaying good with evil is the worst kind of ingratitude (Psalm 35:12; Psalm 109:4–5; Jeremiah 18:20). The second line says that such evil stays in the family: it "will not depart from his house". The phrase recalls Nathan's word to David after Uriah, who had served him loyally, was killed: "the sword will not go away from your house, ever" (2 Samuel 12:10). The New Testament goes further and forbids repaying evil even for evil (Romans 12:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:15; 1 Peter 3:9; compare Proverbs 20:22 and 24:29).
r: Psalm 35:12; Psalm 109:4–5; Jeremiah 18:20; 2 Samuel 12:10; 20:22; 24:29; Romans 12:17; 1 Peter 3:9

a: like letting water loose
p: A quarrel starts like a small leak in an irrigation channel. Once it widens, no one can stop the flood.
b: Poter mayim, "one who lets water loose", pictures a breach in a dam, a cistern or the bank of an irrigation ditch. Rashi describes it well: the water finds a small hole in the channel wall, and the hole grows wider and wider. Quarrels work the same way, so the second line tells the reader to "let it go" (netosh, abandon it) before it "breaks out". The rare verb hitgalla' appears elsewhere only in 18:1 and 20:3, both about fools who burst out into quarrels.
orig: פּוֹטֵר מַיִם רֵאשִׁית מָדוֹן (poter mayim reshit madon), 'one who lets out water is the beginning of strife'

a: Declaring the wicked innocent and declaring the righteous guilty
p: 'Justify' is a court word. Paul's claim that God 'justifies the ungodly' (Romans 4:5) stands out against this verse.
b: Matsdiq rasha' means a judge who declares the guilty party in the right, and marshia' tsaddiq one who condemns the innocent. The same pair appears in the Law's rule for judges (Deuteronomy 25:1) and in Isaiah's woe on those who acquit the guilty for a bribe (Isaiah 5:23). In Exodus 23:7 God says, "I will not count the wicked as righteous." Against this background Paul's language in Romans 4:5, that God "justifies the ungodly", was deliberately startling. Paul's answer is that God is both just and the one who justifies, because of Christ's death (Romans 3:25–26). Jewish interpreters read the verse as a straightforward charge to judges.
orig: מַצְדִּיק רָשָׁע וּמַרְשִׁיעַ צַדִּיק (matsdiq rasha' umarshia' tsaddiq)

a: the price of wisdom in a fool's hand
p: Did people pay teachers? The verse may show that wisdom could be bought, though not by someone with no heart for it.
b: The fool has "a price" (mechir) in his hand to "acquire" wisdom (the same verb as "get wisdom" in 4:5–7 and 16:16). Some scholars see a sign that students paid teachers for instruction, as in Egyptian scribal schools and later Greek schools; Sirach invites the uneducated to his house of study and says, "buy wisdom for yourselves without money" (Sirach 51:23–25). Others take the price as a figure of speech. Either way the problem is the fool's lack of "heart" (lev, mind, will): he can pay the fee but has no mind to learn. In Hebrew the heart is the seat of thought and choice, not mainly of feeling.
orig: מְחִיר בְּיַד־כְּסִיל (mechir beyad-kesil), 'a price in the hand of a fool'; וְלֶב־אָיִן (velev-'ayin), 'and there is no heart'

a: a brother is born for the hard days
t: Friend and brother: one person or two?
p: Is the brother the same as the friend (true friends become brothers in trouble) or a contrast (family is for crises)?
b: The two lines can be read as one idea or two. Read as one, a true friend loves at all times and, when trouble comes, proves to be a real brother. Read as a contrast, friends are for every day, but a brother is what you need when hard times hit. 18:24 and 27:10 complicate the picture by preferring a loyal friend to a brother far away. Many Christian readers have heard in the verse an image of Christ, who was born to share human trouble and calls his followers friends and brothers (John 15:13–15; Hebrews 2:11–17), though that is a later reading, not the saying's own point.
orig: וְאָח לְצָרָה יִוָּלֵד (ve'ach letsarah yivvaled), 'and a brother for distress is born'

a: stands good for his neighbor
p: To guarantee someone's debt, you struck hands with the lender. Proverbs warns against it again and again.
b: A surety ('arev) promised to pay a debt if the borrower failed. The deal was sealed with a handshake, "striking the palm" (toqea' kaf). Proverbs warns against it six times (6:1–5; 11:15; 17:18; 20:16; 22:26–27; 27:13), not because it forbids helping a neighbor, which the Law commands (Deuteronomy 15:7–8), but because a guarantor put his own household at risk for a debt he did not control. Judah offered himself as surety for Benjamin (Genesis 43:9; 44:32), and Sirach later takes a gentler line: a good man stands surety for his neighbor (Sirach 29:14–20). "In front of him" (lifne re'ehu) may mean in the neighbor's presence, or on his behalf.
orig: תֹּקֵעַ כָּף עֹרֵב עֲרֻבָּה (toqea' kaf 'orev 'arubbah), 'striking a palm, pledging a pledge'

a: whoever raises his gate high
t: A high gate, or a big mouth?
p: 'Making his opening high' may mean building a showy gate, or opening his mouth in boasting.
b: Magbiah pitcho, "one who makes his opening high", is unclear. Most take petach as a doorway: a man who builds an imposing entrance to show off his wealth invites ruin, either from envy and robbers or from God, who brings down the proud (16:18; Isaiah 2:12–17; Jeremiah 22:13–15). Others note that petach can be the "opening" of the mouth (Micah 7:5; compare Psalm 141:3), so the line means boasting: talking big invites a fall. The first line fits the second reading, since it is about quarreling.
orig: מַגְבִּיהַּ פִּתְחוֹ (magbiah pitcho), 'one who makes high his opening'

a: A glad heart does as much good as a cure
p: The rare word gehah may mean 'healing' or 'the body'. Either way, a cheerful heart helps the whole person.
b: Gehah occurs only here. Most connect it with a verb meaning to heal (Hosea 5:13), so a glad heart "makes healing good". Some, following the Targum ("makes the body fair"), read geviyyah, "body": a glad heart does the body good. The Greek has "a glad heart makes for good health". The second line pictures the opposite: a "stricken spirit" (ruach nekhe'ah, the same phrase as 15:13 and 18:14) dries out the bones, which in Hebrew thought hold a person's strength (3:8; 14:30; 15:30; 16:24). Proverbs treats body and spirit as one: what weighs on the heart weakens the frame.
orig: גֵּהָה (gehah), 'healing' (only here)

a: a bribe slipped from a robe
t: A bribe from the fold of a robe
p: Valuables were carried in the fold of the garment at the chest. A bribe passed from there was hidden from view.
b: The Hebrew says the bribe comes "from the bosom" (mecheq), the fold of the robe above the belt where people carried money and small things (compare 21:14; Exodus 4:6). Passing a gift from there kept it out of sight. The verse condemns the judge or official who takes it "to bend the paths of justice". The Law repeatedly forbids judges to take bribes because "a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise" (Deuteronomy 16:19; Exodus 23:8), and the prophets accuse Israel's leaders of doing just that (Micah 3:11; Isaiah 1:23). Samuel's farewell speech rests on the claim that he never took one (1 Samuel 12:3).
orig: שֹׁחַד מֵחֵק (shochad mecheq), 'a bribe from the bosom'

a: a fool's eyes are off at the far ends of the earth
t: Eyes at the ends of the earth
p: The fool daydreams about distant things and misses wisdom right in front of him.
b: The contrast is between what is near and what is far. For the person of understanding, wisdom is "before his face" (et-pene), close at hand, as Moses says of God's word: "The word is close by you, very close" (Deuteronomy 30:14). The fool's eyes roam to the ends of the earth: he is distracted, restless, always looking for wisdom or excitement somewhere else, or simply unable to fix his attention. Ecclesiastes says the eye is never satisfied with seeing (Ecclesiastes 1:8).

a: nor beating nobles because they are honest
p: The second line can mean flogging nobles 'for their uprightness' or 'beyond what is right'.
b: The first line says it is not good to fine ('anosh, impose a penalty) a righteous person. The second has 'al yosher, which can mean "because of uprightness" (punishing nobles for being honest, as the Plain has it) or "against what is right", "unjustly". Both readings condemn the abuse of power by courts or kings. The Talmud uses the first line to teach that it is improper even for a righteous person to bring punishment on another (Berakhot 7a).
orig: עַל־יֹשֶׁר ('al-yosher), 'for/against uprightness'

a: a person with a cool spirit
t: The cool man and the heated man
p: Egyptian wisdom praised the calm, 'silent' official and warned against the 'heated man'. Proverbs shares the ideal.
b: Egyptian instructions often contrast two types: the "silent man", calm, patient and self-controlled, and the "heated man", hot-tempered and loud. Amenemope compares the heated man in the temple to a tree that withers and is carried off, and the truly silent man to a tree that bears fruit in a garden (chapter 4; compare Psalm 1:3; Jeremiah 17:5–8). Proverbs has the same ideal without the Egyptian terms: the one who holds back words knows something, and the "cool of spirit" has understanding. The written Hebrew has "cool"; the reading tradition has "precious" (see the variant). The Targum's "gentle of spirit" supports the sense of calm. Compare the warning about the hot-tempered man in 22:24.

a: Even a stubborn fool, if he stays silent, is counted as wise
p: Keep quiet and people may think you wise. Later proverbs in many languages say the same.
b: The saying has a wry smile: silence can hide folly, at least for a while. Job told his friends that if they kept silent it would be their wisdom (Job 13:5). Proverbs praises restrained speech often (10:19; 11:12; 13:3), and the Mishnah says, "A fence for wisdom is silence" (Mishnah Avot 3:13). A version of the idea famously attributed to Abraham Lincoln and others, that it is better to stay silent and be thought a fool than to speak and remove all doubt, has no firm source and is a modern echo.

a: The person who cuts himself off is chasing his own wants
p: The Hebrew is obscure. It may describe a loner who rejects advice, or (in the Greek) a man seeking an excuse to drop friends.
b: Leta'avah yevaqqesh nifrad is literally "for desire seeks one who separates himself". Most take it as the Plain does: the person who isolates himself pursues his own wishes and "bursts out" (yitgalla', as in 17:14 and 20:3) against all sound wisdom (tushiyyah, see the note at 2:7). Proverbs prizes counsel (11:14; 15:22), so the loner is a fool. The Greek read ta'anah, "pretext", for ta'avah, "desire": "A man who wants to separate from his friends looks for excuses." Rashi read it of Lot, who separated from Abraham to follow his desire (Genesis 13:11). Medieval and modern readers alike admit the line is uncertain.
orig: לְתַאֲוָה יְבַקֵּשׁ נִפְרָד (leta'avah yevaqqesh nifrad)

a: deep water
p: Are a person's words deep like a hidden well, hard to fathom, or deep like a spring of wisdom? The lines may contrast or match.
b: "Deep waters" can be good or bad. In 20:5 the purpose in a person's heart is deep water that only someone with understanding can draw up; there, depth means hidden. So some read 18:4 as a contrast: ordinary human words are deep and murky, but the spring of wisdom is a clear, flowing brook. Others read the lines as matching: the words of a wise person are deep, flowing and life-giving, like a spring (10:11; 13:14). The Hebrew has no "but", and the Plain keeps the lines side by side. Jesus speaks of streams of living water flowing from the one who believes (John 7:38).

a: Showing favor to the wicked
p: The Hebrew says 'lifting the face of the wicked', an idiom for showing partiality in court.
b: To "lift the face" (s'et pene) of someone is to raise up a person who has bowed before you, that is, to accept him or favor him. In court it means partiality. The Law forbids judges to show it to rich or poor (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 1:17; 16:19), and the same rule returns at 24:23 and 28:21. The second line names the result: the righteous are "turned aside", denied their case. James condemns the same favoritism in the church (James 2:1–9).
orig: שְׂאֵת פְּנֵי־רָשָׁע (s'et pene-rasha'), 'lifting the face of the wicked'

a: A gossip's words are like treats gulped down
p: The rare word for 'treats' suggests morsels swallowed greedily. The same saying returns at 26:22.
b: Mitlahamim appears only here and in 26:22, which repeats this verse word for word. It probably comes from a root meaning to swallow greedily: gossip is like a snack people cannot stop eating. Once swallowed, it goes "down into the inner rooms of the belly" (chadre-vaten), the deepest parts of a person (20:27, 30), where it stays and works. The point is double: people love to hear gossip, and what they hear sticks. The Greek has a different saying here (fear casts down the lazy). The Targum says the slanderer's words bring him down to the depth of Sheol.
orig: כְּמִתְלַהֲמִים (kemitlahamim), 'like things swallowed greedily'

a: The LORD's name is a tower of strength
p: Towers in a city wall were the last refuge in a siege. The LORD's name, his revealed self, is that refuge.
b: A migdal 'oz was a fortified tower, the strongest point of a city, where people fled when the walls fell (Judges 9:51). "The name of the LORD" stands for God himself as he has made himself known and can be called on (Exodus 34:5–7; Psalm 20:1). The righteous "run" into it and are "set on high" (nisgav), lifted out of the enemy's reach, a word that gives the noun "stronghold" in the Psalms (Psalm 9:9; Psalm 18:2). The next verse is a pointed contrast: the rich man's refuge is his wealth, and only "in his imagining" (18:11).
orig: מִגְדַּל־עֹז שֵׁם יְהוָה (migdal-'oz shem YHWH)
r: 18:11; Judges 9:51; Psalm 61:3; Psalm 9:9; Psalm 18:2; Psalm 20:1; Joel 2:32; Romans 10:13

a: A rich man's wealth is a fortress town to him
p: The first line repeats 10:15. Set after 18:10, it contrasts trust in God with trust in money.
b: The first line is word for word the same as 10:15a, and the Plain renders it the same way. In 10:15 it is a plain observation: wealth protects the rich, as poverty ruins the poor. Here, placed right after 18:10, it gains a sharp edge: the righteous run into the LORD's tower, the rich man runs into his money. The second line adds the verdict that the high wall exists "in his own imagining" (bemaskito, a word also used for idol images, Leviticus 26:1). Jesus' parable of the rich fool who built bigger barns makes the same point (Luke 12:16–21).
orig: וּכְחוֹמָה נִשְׂגָּבָה בְּמַשְׂכִּיתוֹ (ukhechomah nisgavah bemaskito), 'and like a high wall in his imagination'

a: Giving a reply before you have heard
p: A basic rule of the court and of conversation. Ben Sira and the Talmud repeat it.
b: The rule applies first to judges and witnesses, who must hear a matter fully before deciding it (Deuteronomy 13:14; 18:17), and then to anyone in conversation. Sirach turns it into advice: do not answer before you have listened, and do not break in while another is speaking (Sirach 11:8). The Talmud cites this verse when it ranks the man who answers before he hears among the worst of nuisances, quoting the book of Ben Sira (Bava Batra 98b). James gives the New Testament form: "quick to hear, slow to speak" (James 1:19).

a: A gift clears a wide path for the one who gives it
p: Mattan is a gift, not the usual word for a bribe. The verse may mean a proper present to a superior, or how bribes work.
b: Visitors to a king or great man brought gifts: Jacob's present for Joseph (Genesis 43:11), the Queen of Sheba's for Solomon (1 Kings 10:2, 10), Abigail's for David (1 Samuel 25:27). Such gifts were expected courtesy, not corruption. The word here is mattan, "gift", not shochad, the bribe that bends justice (17:23). So many readers take the verse as practical advice for a young man entering court life. Others place it with 17:8 and 21:14 as a cool observation that money opens doors, leaving the reader to judge. The saying "a man's gift makes room for him" (KJV) is often quoted today of a person's talent, but the Hebrew means a present.
orig: מַתָּן אָדָם (mattan adam), 'a person's gift'

a: then his neighbor shows up and puts him to the test
p: Courts at the town gate heard both parties. This verse is a basic rule of fair procedure.
b: Legal cases were heard by the elders at the city gate (Ruth 4:1–11; Deuteronomy 21:19). The first speaker always sounds convincing until the other party "comes and examines him" (chaqaro, searches him out), that is, cross-examines. The Law requires judges to "inquire thoroughly" (Deuteronomy 19:18) and to hear the case between a man and his neighbor fairly (Deuteronomy 1:16). The written Hebrew has "his neighbor will come" (yavo); the reading tradition adds "and" (uva). The meaning does not change.
orig: וּבָא־רֵעֵהוּ וַחֲקָרוֹ (uva-re'ehu vachaqaro), 'and his neighbor comes and examines him'

a: The lot brings quarrels to an end
p: When strong parties could not agree, the lot decided, and both accepted it as God's choice.
b: This follows from 16:33: if the outcome of the lot is the LORD's, then the lot can end a dispute that would otherwise be settled by force. It "parts the powerful", separating strong rivals before they come to blows. Israel divided its land by lot to prevent quarrels among the tribes (Numbers 26:55–56; Joshua 14:2), and the priests divided their duties the same way (1 Chronicles 24:5, 31; 1 Chronicles 25:8).

a: An offended brother is harder to take than a strong town
p: The Hebrew lacks a verb, and the Plain supplies 'harder to take'. The Greek praises brothers who help each other.
b: The Hebrew is literally "A brother offended, than a strong city". English versions supply "is harder to win than" or something similar, and the second line supports that: quarrels shut people out like the bars of a fortress gate. The verb nifsha', "offended" or "wronged", is the root of pesha', rebellion. The Greek, followed by the Latin, read a different word, perhaps nosha', "helped": "A brother helped by a brother is like a strong, high city." Rashi gives the examples of Lot and Esau, brothers whose quarrels never healed. See the variant.
orig: אָח נִפְשָׁע מִקִּרְיַת־עֹז (ach nifsha' miqqiryat-'oz)

a: Death and life are in the tongue's hand
p: Literally 'in the hand of the tongue'. The rabbis asked: does the tongue have a hand? Yes, because it can kill.
b: The Hebrew image is that the tongue holds death and life "in its hand", that is, in its power. The Talmud plays on the picture: just as a hand can kill, so can a tongue, and even at a distance, like an arrow (Arakhin 15b, quoting Jeremiah 9:8). Rava adds that a person can gain life through the tongue, by speaking rightly and studying Torah, or death, through malicious speech. "Those who love it" are those who love to talk, and they will live with the results, whether sweet or bitter. James builds a whole section on the tongue's power (James 3:1–12). Note: this is not a promise that speaking a wish makes it happen, a claim some modern teachers attach to the verse.
orig: מָוֶת וְחַיִּים בְּיַד־לָשׁוֹן (mavet vechayyim beyad-lashon)

a: The one who finds a wife has found something good
p: The same Hebrew as Wisdom's promise in 8:35b. Finding a wife, like finding wisdom, brings the LORD's favor.
b: The Hebrew is the same as the second half of what Wisdom says of herself in 8:35: "The one who finds me has found life, / and he draws favor from the LORD." The Plain renders the two alike. Finding a wife is like finding wisdom, a gift of God's favor (19:14; 31:10), and the saying answers Genesis 2:18, "It is not good for the man to be by himself". Other sayings show that Proverbs did not think every marriage good (19:13; 21:9, 19; 25:24), and the Greek reads "a good wife" and adds a saying against sending away a good wife (the Greek 18:22a); see the variant. The Talmud reports that in the land of Israel a new husband was asked, "Matsa or motse?": was his marriage this verse ("finds", matsa), or Ecclesiastes 7:26 ("I find", motse, a woman more bitter than death)? (Berakhot 8a).

a: Someone with lots of friends can be broken by them
p: A pun: re'im 'friends' and hitro'ea 'be broken' sound alike. The KJV's 'shew himself friendly' reads the verb differently.
b: The first line plays on sound: 'ish re'im lehitro'ea, "a man of friends is for being shattered" (from ra'a', to break). Many casual companions can bring a person to ruin. The KJV took the verb from ra'ah, "to associate with", giving "A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly", a popular saying that is a mistranslation of this line. The second line names the alternative, the one who "loves" (ohev) and "clings" (davaq, the verb of Genesis 2:24 and Ruth 1:14) closer than a brother. David and Jonathan are the Bible's model (1 Samuel 18:1–3). The Talmud warns against filling one's house with too many friends (Berakhot 63a).
orig: אִישׁ רֵעִים לְהִתְרֹעֵעַ ('ish re'im lehitro'ea')

a: A poor man living with integrity is better
p: The first line returns almost word for word in 28:6, where the contrast is with a crooked rich man.
b: 28:6 repeats the first line and changes the second: there the poor man of integrity is better than "one who is crooked in his ways, though he is rich". The contrast here, with a fool of twisted lips, is odd, since a fool is not the obvious opposite of a poor man. The Targum has "one who twists his ways" here, as in 28:6, while the Hebrew and the Vulgate keep "lips" and "fool". The point may be that a fool with a smooth tongue often gets ahead, and the honest poor man is still better. "Integrity" (tom) is wholeness, the quality God praises in Job (Job 1:1; Job 2:3). The Greek lacks 18:23–19:2.
orig: טוֹב־רָשׁ הוֹלֵךְ בְּתֻמּוֹ (tov-rash holekh betummo), 'better a poor man walking in his integrity'

a: rush along on your feet and you miss the mark
p: The verb chata' means both 'miss the mark' and 'sin'. Haste without knowledge leads a person astray.
b: Chote' is the ordinary word for sinning, but its root meaning is to miss a target, as the left-handed slingers of Benjamin could sling a stone at a hair and not miss (Judges 20:16). The first line uses nefesh for desire or eagerness: zeal without knowledge is not good. Paul says something close about Israel's zeal for God, which was not based on knowledge (Romans 10:2). The two lines together warn the eager young: enthusiasm needs the patience to learn first.
orig: וְאָץ בְּרַגְלַיִם חוֹטֵא (ve'ats beraglayim chote'), 'and one hasty with feet misses/sins'

a: he is furious at the LORD in his heart
p: A person ruins his own life by folly, then rages at God. The saying names a common human reaction.
b: The verb yiz'af means to rage or storm. A person's own folly "overturns" his way (tesalleph, the word for subverting or twisting in 13:6 and 22:12), and then he blames the LORD. Adam's first excuse is the classic case: "The woman! You set her at my side" (Genesis 3:12). The Greek puts it pointedly: "he blames God in his heart." Sirach warns: "Do not say, 'It was the Lord's doing that I fell away'" (Sirach 15:11), and James says God tempts no one (James 1:13–14). Job's protests are different: the book tells the reader that his suffering was not caused by his folly (Job 1:8).
orig: וְעַל־יְהוָה יִזְעַף לִבּוֹ (ve'al-YHWH yiz'af libbo)

a: He runs after them with words, and they are gone
p: The only three-line saying in this stretch, and its third line is hard. The Greek has two extra couplets here.
b: The first two lines are clear: a poor man's brothers hate him, and his friends keep further away still. The third line is literally "one who pursues words, not they" (Ketiv lo', "not") or "they are his" (Qere lo). It may mean that he chases them with pleas and they are gone, or that he chases after mere words, promises that come to nothing. Many scholars think a line has dropped out, since the Greek has three couplets here: one on the brother who hates the poor, then "Good understanding draws near to those who know it, and a man of sense will find it", and "He who does much evil completes wickedness, and he who provokes with words will not escape". That last line seems to render the same Hebrew as this third line.
orig: מְרַדֵּף אֲמָרִים לֹא־הֵמָּה (meradef amarim lo'-hemmah)

a: far less a slave ruling princes
p: Proverbs reflects the social order of its day. A slave ruling princes was a sign of the world turned upside down.
b: Ancient wisdom often lists reversals of social order as disasters: a slave becoming king (30:21–22), servants on horseback while princes walk (Ecclesiastes 10:5–7). The Egyptian Admonitions of Ipuwer describe a time of chaos when the poor have become rich and officials are in rags. Such sayings come from a court setting that took rank for granted, and modern readers notice it. Proverbs is not consistent here, though: 17:2 praises the capable servant who takes the disgraceful son's place. The Bible also tells of slaves who rose to rule wisely, Joseph above all (Genesis 41:39–43), and Paul's teaching that in Christ there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28) points another way.
orig: לְעֶבֶד מְשֹׁל בְּשָׂרִים (le'eved meshol besarim)

a: his honor lies in letting a wrong go by
p: To 'pass over' a wrong is what God does in forgiving (Micah 7:18). Here it is a person's glory.
b: "Pass over" ('avor 'al) a transgression is the phrase Micah uses of God: "Who is a God like you, who forgives guilt and passes over the rebellion of the remnant of his inheritance?" (Micah 7:18). Patience and forbearance are part of God's own name (Exodus 34:6), and Proverbs makes them a person's honor too. Compare 12:16 ("the shrewd man keeps an insult covered") and 17:9. Jesus teaches unlimited forgiveness of a brother (Matthew 18:21–22).
orig: וְתִפְאַרְתּוֹ עֲבֹר עַל־פָּשַׁע (vetif'arto 'avor 'al-pasha')

a: a drip that never stops
p: Flat roofs of packed earth leaked in the rainy season. The constant drip is a picture of endless quarreling.
b: Houses had flat roofs of beams covered with branches and packed clay, which had to be rolled after rain and still leaked (Ecclesiastes 10:18). A "continual dripping" (delef tored) in the winter rains was maddening and slowly ruinous. 27:15 repeats the image at length. The sayings on the quarrelsome wife (19:13; 21:9, 19; 25:24; 27:15–16) were written for men, in a book addressed to sons; modern readers rightly note that a book written for daughters might have said the same of quarrelsome husbands. Proverbs balances them with high praise for the sensible wife (12:4; 18:22; 19:14; 31:10–31).
orig: וְדֶלֶף טֹרֵד מִדְיְנֵי אִשָּׁה (vedelef tored midyene ishshah), 'a continual dripping, the quarrels of a wife'

a: a wife with good sense comes from the LORD
p: Property passes down from parents, but a good wife is the LORD's gift. In practice, parents arranged marriages.
b: The contrast is not between human and divine action in general but between what can be planned and what cannot. Houses and wealth come by inheritance (nachalat avot); a sensible wife (ishshah maskalet) comes from the LORD. Parents arranged most marriages, yet the outcome was still seen as God's gift, as when Abraham's servant prays to find Rebekah (Genesis 24:12–14, 50). Compare 18:22. The word maskalet is the same root as the "servant with good sense" in 17:2 and as Abigail's "good sense" (1 Samuel 25:3).
orig: וּמֵיְהוָה אִשָּׁה מַשְׂכָּלֶת (umeYHWH ishshah maskalet)

a: take no care for your ways and you will die
p: The man who 'despises his ways' may be careless of his own conduct, or may despise God's ways.
b: The first line is clear: whoever keeps the command (mitsvah, the father's or God's) keeps his life. The second has bozeh derakhav, "one who despises his ways", that is, one careless about his own conduct. Rashi: he "does not take heed to weigh them". Proverbs often sets the commandment and life side by side (4:4; 7:2), and the careless road and death (15:10). On the written "will be put to death" against the read "will die", see the variant.
orig: בּוֹזֵה דְרָכָיו יָמוּת (bozeh derakhav yamut); Ketiv יוּמָת (yumat), 'will be put to death'

a: a loan made to the LORD
p: Kindness to the poor is a loan to God, and God repays. Rabbi Yochanan said no one could say it if the Bible had not.
b: The verb malveh is the ordinary word for lending money. Giving to the poor puts God in the giver's debt, and he "will pay him back" (yeshallem). The Talmud records Rabbi Yochanan's comment: "Were it not written in the verse, it would be impossible to say it," since 22:7 says the borrower is the lender's servant (Bava Batra 10a). Jesus teaches that what is done for the least of his brothers is done for him (Matthew 25:40), and that giving to those who cannot repay will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous (Luke 14:13–14). The Greek has "he who has pity on a poor man lends to God".
orig: מַלְוֵה יְהוָה חוֹנֵן דָּל (malveh YHWH chonen dal), 'one who lends to the LORD is one who is gracious to the poor'

a: do not set yourself on bringing about his death
p: A warning against discipline so harsh it kills, or a warning that failing to discipline will lead to the son's death?
b: The literal second line is "and to his death do not lift up your soul (desire)". Readers take it in two opposite ways. (1) A limit on punishment: discipline your son, but do not let anger carry you so far that you want him dead. Rashi: "Do not deal him a lethal blow." The Greek, "do not be lifted up in your soul to insolence", reads the same way. (2) A warning against neglect: discipline him while there is hope, for if you do not, you are a party to his death (compare 23:13–14, where the rod saves from Sheol; Deuteronomy 21:18–21). Both readings assume physical discipline was normal; the first is a check on it. On the rod in Proverbs, see 13:24.
orig: וְאֶל־הֲמִיתוֹ אַל־תִּשָּׂא נַפְשֶׁךָ (ve'el-hamito al-tissa nafshekha)

a: A hothead must pay the fine
p: The written text has a rare word; the reading tradition has 'great of rage'. A hothead keeps getting into trouble.
b: The reading tradition (Qere) has gedal-chemah, "great of rage", a hothead. The written consonants (Ketiv) are g-r-l, which make no clear sense; they could be read goral, "lot", and some guess at a word meaning "rough". The man "bears the penalty" ('onesh, a fine, as in 17:26). The second line warns the would-be rescuer: if you pay his way out, he will only do it again, and you will have to rescue him again. Proverbs does not forbid mercy; it warns that shielding a person from the results of his temper teaches him nothing.
orig: גְּדָל־חֵמָה (gedal-chemah) Qere; Ketiv גרל (g-r-l)

a: the LORD's purpose is the one that holds
p: A twin of 16:9. Many human plans, one divine purpose. Isaiah and the Psalms say the same of nations.
b: The heart holds "many plans" (machashavot), but the LORD's "counsel" or "purpose" ('atsah) "will stand" (taqum). The Psalms and Isaiah say this on the scale of nations (Psalm 33:10–11; Isaiah 14:24–27; Isaiah 46:10). Gamaliel's advice to the council in Acts rests on the same idea: if this work is of human origin it will fail, but if it is from God you cannot stop it (Acts 5:38–39). Compare 16:1, 9; 20:24; 21:30.
orig: וַעֲצַת יְהוָה הִיא תָקוּם (va'atsat YHWH hi taqum)

a: What makes a man desirable is his loyal love
p: Hard Hebrew. It may mean that kindness is what people look for in a person, or that a man's greed is his shame.
b: Ta'avat adam chasdo could mean "what is desired in a person is his loyal love" (the Plain, with most modern versions), or "a person's desire is his kindness", that is, his generosity reflects what he truly wants. A third view takes chesed in its rare sense "shame" (Leviticus 20:17) and reads "a man's greed is his shame". The second line then follows: better to be poor (and honest) than a liar who promises loyalty and does not give it. The Greek renders "Mercy is a fruit for a man, and a righteous poor man is better than a rich liar".
orig: תַּאֲוַת אָדָם חַסְדּוֹ (ta'avat adam chasdo)

a: The lazy one sinks his hand into the bowl
p: A comic picture. Food was eaten from a shared bowl with the hand. The lazy one cannot finish the motion.
b: Diners scooped food from a common dish with bread or the hand (Matthew 26:23). The lazy one ('atsel) gets as far as burying his hand in the dish but cannot be bothered to bring it back to his mouth. The exaggeration is meant to make people laugh, and laughter teaches. 26:15 repeats the picture and adds that it wears him out. The lazy one is a stock figure in this collection (10:26; 13:4; 15:19; 20:4; 21:25; 22:13; 26:13–16), as in the Egyptian satires on idle scribes.
orig: טָמַן עָצֵל יָדוֹ בַּצַּלָּחַת (taman 'atsel yado batsallachat)

a: When a mocker is beaten, a naive person gets shrewd
p: The mocker himself will not learn, but the naive who watch will. Proverbs ranks who can be taught.
b: This saying and its near twin 21:11 sort people by teachability. The mocker (lets) scorns correction and will not change (9:7–8; 13:1; 15:12), so beating him does him no good, but the naive (peti), who are still open to influence, see the result and learn to be shrewd. The discerning (navon) need only words. The Law's punishments were meant to work the same way: "all Israel will hear and be afraid" (Deuteronomy 13:11; Deuteronomy 19:20). Paul tells Timothy to rebuke persistent sinners in front of everyone, so that the rest will be afraid too (1 Timothy 5:20).

a: A son who mistreats his father and chases away his mother
p: Children were their parents' only pension. A son who drove out his widowed mother left her with nothing.
b: In Israel parents in old age depended on their children, and the command to honor father and mother (Exodus 20:12) included supporting them. Meshadded means to ruin or violently mistreat, perhaps by seizing the father's property; yavriach means to drive away, perhaps the widowed mother from the family house. Jesus attacked a custom that let sons dedicate to God the money owed to their parents (Mark 7:9–13). The Law punished striking or cursing a parent with death (Exodus 21:15, 17; compare Proverbs 20:20). "Shames and humiliates" are a common pair (mevish umachpir), as in 13:5.
orig: מְשַׁדֶּד־אָב יַבְרִיחַ אֵם (meshadded-av yavriach em)

a: My son, stop listening to discipline
p: A command to stop listening, meant ironically: if you want to wander from knowledge, just stop listening.
b: The verse is literally "Cease, my son, to listen to discipline, to stray from words of knowledge." Read flatly it tells the son to stop listening, which cannot be the point. Most read it as irony (go ahead, stop listening, if your goal is to wander off) or as a condensed warning (stop listening to discipline and you will stray). Rashi calls it elliptical and reads "cease straying from words of knowledge, so as to hear discipline"; the Vulgate turns it round, "do not cease to hear", and the Targum makes it two commands, "hear" and "do not stray". This is the only "my son" in chapters 10–22:16; the address is common in chapters 1–9 and returns at 23:15 and 24:13.
orig: חֲדַל־בְּנִי לִשְׁמֹעַ מוּסָר (chadal-beni lishmoa' musar)

a: Wine is a mocker, and beer is a rowdy
p: Wine and beer are pictured as two of the book's bad characters: the mocker and the brawler. Both were ordinary drinks.
b: Yayin is grape wine. Shekhar is any other fermented drink, above all barley beer, the everyday drink of Egypt and Mesopotamia; distilled spirits did not exist. The proverb does not condemn the drinks so much as personify them. Wine is a lets, the "mocker" who scorns correction throughout Proverbs (1:22; 9:7–8; 19:25, 29), and beer is homeh, "noisy, rowdy", the word used of the loud woman Folly (9:13). Drink makes a person behave like them. The Vulgate: "wine is a wanton thing, and drunkenness riotous". The Greek: "wine is licentious and drunkenness insolent".
orig: לֵץ הַיַּיִן הֹמֶה שֵׁכָר (lets hayyayin homeh shekhar)

a: anyone who reels under their power is not wise
p: The saying condemns being led astray by drink. Jews and Christians have read it as a call to moderation or abstinence.
b: The verb shagah means to stagger or go astray, and it is the word used of being "intoxicated" with a wife's love in 5:19–20; it can describe a drunk's reeling or a life that wanders off. The proverb faults the person who is "led astray by it", not drink as such. Elsewhere the Bible praises wine that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15), Jesus made wine at Cana (John 2:1–11) and Paul advises a little for the stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), while Nazirites and Rechabites abstained (Numbers 6:1–4; Jeremiah 35). The Talmud reads Psalm 104:15 in the same balanced way: a moderate amount gladdens, too much makes a person crazy (Sanhedrin 70a). On how churches apply it, see the chapter page.
orig: וְכָל־שֹׁגֶה בּוֹ לֹא יֶחְכָּם (vekhol-shogeh bo lo yechkam)

a: The dread a king inspires growls like a young lion
p: Nearly the same as 19:12a. Royal power is pictured as a lion, and provoking it is a sin against one's own life.
b: "Dread" (emah) is the terror a king inspires; 19:12 has "fury" (za'af) in the same line. Kings in the ancient Near East often compared themselves to lions, and the lion hunt was a royal sport in Assyrian art. "Provokes him" (mit'abbero) is to make him angry. "Puts your life at risk" is literally "sins against his life": the word chote' again carries its root sense of missing the mark (19:2). Compare 16:14 and the advice of Ecclesiastes 8:2–4.

a: The lazy one does not plow when winter comes
p: Fields were plowed after the first autumn rains. The lazy one stays in out of the cold and has no harvest.
b: The Hebrew mechoref means "from autumn/winter" or "because of the winter": the plowing season came after the early rains of October and November, when the ground softened, in cold and wet weather. The Gezer calendar, an early Hebrew inscription, lists the farming months, with sowing after the olive harvest. The man who will not plow then "asks" at harvest (sha'al, perhaps "begs") and there is nothing. Compare the ant that stores in summer (6:6–8) and the lazy person's field in 24:30–34.
orig: מֵחֹרֶף עָצֵל לֹא־יַחֲרֹשׁ (mechoref 'atsel lo-yacharosh)

a: A plan in someone's heart is deep water
p: A person's real intent lies deep, like water in a well. An understanding man has a bucket long enough to draw it up.
b: Water in a deep well or cistern could only be reached by letting a bucket down on a rope and hauling it up (dalah, used of Moses drawing water in Exodus 2:16, 19). A person's real purpose ('etsah) lies deep in the heart, and a discerning person can draw it out by patient questions. 18:4 uses the same picture of deep waters for a wise man's words. The verse can be read two ways: the wise draws out others' plans, or his own.
orig: מַיִם עֲמֻקִּים עֵצָה בְלֶב־אִישׁ (mayim 'amuqqim 'etsah velev-ish)

a: but someone truly faithful, who can find?
p: Many announce their own loyalty; a faithful person is rare. 31:10 asks the same question about a capable wife.
b: The question "who can find?" (mi yimtsa') returns in 31:10, about a woman of strength. A person "calls out" (yiqra') his own chesed, boasting of his loyalty, but someone "of faithfulness" (ish emunim), who does what he promises, is hard to find. Psalm 12:1 laments that "the faithful have disappeared from among humankind", and Jeremiah is sent to search Jerusalem for one person who acts justly (Jeremiah 5:1). The Greek reads the first line differently: "A merciful man is a great and precious thing".
orig: וְאִישׁ אֱמוּנִים מִי יִמְצָא (ve'ish emunim mi yimtsa')

a: how happy his children are after him!
p: A righteous life is an inheritance. Children benefit from a parent's integrity.
b: "How happy" (ashre) is the word that opens Psalm 1. The righteous man "walks in his integrity" (tom), as in 19:1, and his children are blessed after him. Psalm 37:25–26 and Psalm 112:2 say the same. Israel's law balanced this with the rule that each person dies for his own sin (Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18:20), but the good name, the training and the goodwill a parent leaves stay with the children (13:22; 14:26).

a: When a king takes his seat on the judgment throne
p: In Israel the king was the highest court. His eye was meant to 'winnow' evil from the land.
b: The king's "throne of judgment" (kisse-din) was the final court of appeal, as when the two women came before Solomon (1 Kings 3:16–28) and Absalom won hearts by promising better justice (2 Samuel 15:2–6). Solomon built "the throne porch, where he would give judgments" (1 Kings 7:7). "Sifts out" (mezareh) is the word for winnowing grain, tossing it so the wind carries off the chaff; 20:26 uses the same picture. A just king sees through deceit, much as the LORD's eyes do (15:3).
orig: מְזָרֶה בְעֵינָיו כָּל־רָע (mezareh ve'enav kol-ra')

a: I am pure of my sin
p: A rhetorical question with an obvious answer: nobody. The Bible says it many times.
b: No one can say he has made his heart clean. Solomon says at the dedication of the temple that "there is no human being who never sins" (1 Kings 8:46), and Ecclesiastes 7:20 that on earth there is not one righteous human who does good and never sins. Job's friend Eliphaz asks whether a mortal can be pure before his maker (Job 4:17). Psalm 51:10 asks God to create a clean heart, since a person cannot make one. 1 John 1:8 warns that if we claim to have no sin we are leading ourselves astray, and Paul gathers such verses into the claim that all have sinned (Romans 3:9–23).
orig: זִכִּיתִי לִבִּי טָהַרְתִּי מֵחַטָּאתִי (zikkiti libbi taharti mechatta'ti)
r: 1 Kings 8:46; Ecclesiastes 7:20; Job 4:17; Job 15:14; Psalm 51:10; Psalm 143:2; Romans 3:23; 1 John 1:8

a: One weight and another, one measure and another
p: A cheating merchant kept a heavy set of stones for buying and a light one for selling. The LORD hates both.
b: Before coins, silver was weighed on a balance against stone weights, and grain was measured in an efah basket. The Hebrew is "stone and stone, efah and efah": two different sets, one for buying and one for selling. Archaeologists have found many inscribed shekel weights from Judah whose actual masses vary. The Law forbids it (Deuteronomy 25:13–16; Leviticus 19:35–36), the prophets attack it (Amos 8:5; Micah 6:11), and Proverbs returns to it three times (11:1; 16:11; 20:23). Amenemope also warns at length against tampering with the scales and the grain measure (his chapters 16 and 17).
orig: אֶבֶן וָאֶבֶן אֵיפָה וְאֵיפָה (even va'even efah ve'efah)

a: Even a boy shows who he is by what he does
p: Even a young person reveals his character by his actions. The verb may also mean that he 'disguises' himself.
b: The verb yitnakker normally means "make oneself known" or "is recognized", and that is how most read it: even a young person (na'ar) shows by what he does whether his conduct is pure. The same root can mean to disguise oneself (1 Kings 14:5–6), and a few read the verse as a warning that even a boy can put on a good act. Jesus' saying "it is from their fruit that you will know them" (Matthew 7:20) makes the first point. On na'ar, see 22:6.
orig: גַּם בְּמַעֲלָלָיו יִתְנַכֶּר־נָעַר (gam bema'alalav yitnakker-na'ar)

a: "It's junk, it's junk," says the buyer
p: A sketch of the marketplace. The buyer runs down the goods to get a low price, then goes off boasting of his bargain.
b: Prices in the ancient market were set by haggling. The buyer says ra' ra', "bad, bad", to beat the seller down, and once he has paid, he "goes his way" and boasts (yithallal). The saying observes without stating a moral, but the reader sees the dishonesty. The Talmud uses it in a discussion of a buyer's rights when goods are bought by sample (Bava Batra 84a). The Greek lacks 20:14–19.
orig: רַע רַע יֹאמַר הַקּוֹנֶה (ra' ra' yomar haqqoneh)

a: coral in plenty
p: The word peninim is a precious red stone or coral, possibly pearls. Proverbs uses it for the worth of wisdom.
b: Peninim appear as a measure of wisdom's worth (3:15; 8:11) and of the capable wife's (31:10). Lamentations 4:7 says the princes' bodies were redder than peninim, which suggests red coral, from the Red Sea; the Plain says "red coral", as in 3:15 and 31:10. The older reading "rubies" (KJV) and the guess "pearls" are also found. Here gold and many peninim exist, but lips that speak knowledge are the rarer "vessel of value" (keli yeqar).
orig: וְרָב־פְּנִינִים (verav-peninim)

a: Take the garment of a man who stands good for an outsider
p: Repeated almost exactly in 27:13. A man who backs a stranger's loan must expect to lose his cloak.
b: This is the fourth warning against surety in Proverbs (6:1–5; 11:15; 17:18; 22:26–27; 27:13 repeats this verse). The lender is told: take the guarantor's garment as a pledge, since he was foolish enough to vouch for an outsider. The Law said a poor man's cloak taken in pledge had to be returned before nightfall, since he slept in it (Exodus 22:26–27; Deuteronomy 24:12–13), but this verse is advice, not law. On the reading "foreign woman" or "foreigners" in the second line, see the variant. The Talmud uses the verse in a discussion of guarantors (Bava Batra 173b).
orig: לְקַח־בִּגְדוֹ כִּי־עָרַב זָר (leqach-bigdo ki-'arav zar)

a: his mouth gets filled with grit
p: Gain by fraud tastes sweet at first and turns to gravel in the mouth.
b: Chatsats is gravel or grit, as in Lamentations 3:16, where the poet says God has broken his teeth on gravel. Bread baked on the ground or ground in stone mills often had grit in it, and the image would be familiar. The pattern of sweet beginnings and bitter ends runs through Proverbs: stolen water (9:17–18), the strange woman's honeyed lips that end bitter as wormwood (5:3–4). Compare also Job's friend Zophar on the wicked man's food turning to venom in his stomach (Job 20:12–15).
orig: וְאַחַר יִמָּלֵא־פִיהוּ חָצָץ (ve'achar yimmale-fihu chatsats)

a: so make war with skilled steering
p: The word for guidance comes from steering a ship. Kings did not go to war without counsel.
b: Tachbulot, "steering" or skilled guidance, comes from chovel, a sailor (Ezekiel 27:8; Jonah 1:6), and is one of the skills the book promises (1:5). Israel's kings took counsel before battle (1 Kings 22:5–28; 2 Samuel 17:1–14, where the choice between Ahithophel's and Hushai's advice decides Absalom's war). Jesus uses the example of a king who sits down to consider whether his ten thousand can meet twenty thousand (Luke 14:31). Compare 11:14; 15:22; 24:6.
orig: וּבְתַחְבֻּלוֹת עֲשֵׂה מִלְחָמָה (uvetachbulot 'aseh milchamah)

a: your lamp will go out when the dark is deepest
p: A lamp burned through the night in a home, a picture of life and of a family line. Cursing parents puts it out.
b: A small oil lamp was kept burning through the night in Israelite homes, so a lamp going out stood for death and the end of a household (13:9; 24:20; Job 18:5–6). "The pupil of darkness" (ishon choshekh, as written; the reading tradition has eshun, "time") is the blackest point of night; 7:9 uses the same word, "in the black of night". Cursing (meqallel, treating as light, contemptible) a father or mother carried the death penalty under the Law (Exodus 21:17; Leviticus 20:9), and Jesus cites that law (Matthew 15:4).
orig: יִדְעַךְ נֵרוֹ בֶּאֱשׁוּן חֹשֶׁךְ (yid'akh nero be'eshun choshekh)

a: Property grabbed in a hurry at the start
p: Literally an 'inheritance hurried' (Qere) or 'gotten by greed' (Ketiv). The prodigal son comes to mind.
b: The reading tradition (Qere) has mevohelet, "hastened", while the written text (Ketiv) has mevuchelet, perhaps "gotten by greed" (compare Zechariah 11:8). The word nachalah is an inheritance, so the picture may be an heir who grabs his share early, perhaps by pushing out a parent (19:26). Jesus' parable of the younger son who asked for his share of the estate and wasted it tells the same story (Luke 15:11–13). Compare 13:11; 28:20, 22.
orig: נַחֲלָה מְבֹהֶלֶת בָּרִאשֹׁנָה (nachalah mevohelet bari'shonah)

a: Do not say, "I will get even for the evil."
p: Do not take revenge; wait for the LORD. Paul makes the same point, quoting Proverbs 25 and Deuteronomy.
b: The verb ashallemah, "I will repay", is the same as in 19:17, where God repays kindness. Here the reader is to leave repayment of evil to God and "wait for" (qavveh) him, the patient trust of the Psalms (Psalm 27:14; Psalm 37:34). The Law forbids taking vengeance or bearing a grudge (Leviticus 19:18), and Proverbs 24:29 and 25:21–22 go further, to feeding one's enemy. Paul tells believers to pay no one back evil for evil and not to take revenge themselves, but to give way to God's wrath (Romans 12:17–21); compare 1 Thessalonians 5:15 and 1 Peter 3:9. The Greek has "I will avenge myself on my enemy".
orig: אַל־תֹּאמַר אֲשַׁלְּמָה־רָע (al-tomar ashallemah-ra')
r: 24:29; 25:21–22; Leviticus 19:18; Deuteronomy 32:35; Psalm 37:34; Romans 12:17–21; 1 Thessalonians 5:15; 1 Peter 3:9

a: what human, then, can figure out his own path?
p: A person's steps are from God; he cannot fully understand his own way. Jeremiah says it almost word for word.
b: "A man's steps come from the LORD" is close to Psalm 37:23, "It is the LORD who makes a man's steps firm". Jeremiah prays that a human's road is not in his own hands, and that no one walking can set his own steps (Jeremiah 10:23). The two words for person differ: gever, a strong man, in the first line and adam, a mere human, in the second. The saying does not tell the reader to stop planning (20:18) but to plan humbly. Compare 16:1, 9; 19:21.

a: It is a snare to blurt out, "This is holy!"
p: To declare something 'holy', dedicated to God, in a burst of feeling, and only then think about the cost, is a trap.
b: A person could vow an animal, a field or money to the sanctuary by declaring it qodesh, "holy" (Leviticus 27). Once said, the vow bound him. Ecclesiastes warns against delay in paying a vow, and says it is better not to vow at all than to vow and fail to pay (Ecclesiastes 5:4–6), and the Law says it is no sin to refrain from vowing (Deuteronomy 23:21–23). Jephthah's vow is the Bible's terrible example (Judges 11:30–40). The verb yala' is rare; it may mean to say rashly. The Talmud, by wordplay on yala' and the word for cheek, reads it as a warning against striking a fellow Jew, an affront to God (Sanhedrin 58b).
orig: מוֹקֵשׁ אָדָם יָלַע קֹדֶשׁ (moqesh adam yala' qodesh)
