a: and runs the wheel over them
p: Grain was threshed with a sledge or cart wheel, then winnowed. A wise king does both to the wicked.
b: To thresh, farmers drove a sledge studded with stones, or a cart with wheels, over the sheaves on a threshing floor, and then winnowed (mezareh) the result with a fork so the wind blew the chaff away. Isaiah 28:27–28 mentions the cart wheel used for threshing. The picture is of a king who separates the wicked and crushes their power, not of torture. Rashi takes the wise king as God, who turned the wheel of Pharaoh's chariots against him. Compare 20:8.
orig: וַיָּשֶׁב עֲלֵיהֶם אוֹפָן (vayyashev 'alehem ofan)

a: The human breath is the LORD's lamp
p: The breath God gave the first human (Genesis 2:7) is pictured as a lamp that lights up a person's inner self for God.
b: Nishmat adam, the human breath, is the breath of life God breathed into Adam (Genesis 2:7; Job 32:8). It is here God's lamp, "searching" (chofes, the word for searching with a lamp, Zephaniah 1:12) every "inner room of the belly", the hidden depths of a person. Ancient readers took it as conscience, or the spirit, through which God sees and judges. Rashi: the soul within a person testifies about him in judgment. In the Talmud Rav Tanchum reasons that a lamp may be put out for a sick person, since a human soul is also called the LORD's lamp (Shabbat 30b), and the soul is called God's lamp again in Shabbat 32a. Paul's "the person's own spirit within him" (1 Corinthians 2:11) is close.
orig: נֵר יְהוָה נִשְׁמַת אָדָם (ner YHWH nishmat adam)

a: Loyal love and faithfulness stand guard over a king
t: The throne held up by loyalty
p: Chesed and emet, the pair that describes God (Exodus 34:6), protect a king's rule.
b: Chesed ve'emet, loyal love and faithfulness, are the two qualities of the LORD's name (Exodus 34:6) and the pair from 3:3 and 16:6. In royal theology they are the guardians of the Davidic throne (Psalm 61:6–7; Psalm 89:14, 24), and Isaiah foresees that "by loyal love a throne will be made firm", with someone sitting on it faithfully (Isaiah 16:5). The Greek turns the second line into "they will surround his throne with righteousness", like 16:12; 25:5.
orig: חֶסֶד וֶאֱמֶת יִצְּרוּ־מֶלֶךְ (chesed ve'emet yitsseru-melekh)

a: old men's beauty is their gray hair
p: Each age has its glory: strength for the young, gray hair and experience for the old.
b: Gray hair (sevah) is "a crown of beauty, / found by those who walk in righteousness" in 16:31; the Plain uses "gray hair" for sevah in both verses. The Law commands rising before the gray-haired (Leviticus 19:32). Ecclesiastes 12:1 urges the young to remember their creator before old age comes. The Greek makes it "wisdom is an ornament to young men", turning strength into wisdom. 1 John 2:13–14 addresses "young men" as strong and "fathers" as knowing.

a: Bruising wounds scour evil away
p: A hard verse. Physical punishment is said to 'scour' evil, reaching the inner self. The words are uncertain.
b: Chabburot petsa' are welts and wounds; tamriq (Qere tamruq) is a scouring or cleansing, as with ointment or polish (Esther 2:3, 12; Jeremiah 46:4 has the verb for polishing). The second line, "blows ... the inner rooms of the belly", echoes 20:27 and 18:8. The saying claims that punishment reaches the inner person and purges evil. Rashi reads it as a warning instead: one who pours himself into sin comes to wounds. Compare 19:29; 26:3. On physical discipline, see 13:24 and 22:15.
orig: חַבֻּרוֹת פֶּצַע תַּמְרִיק בְּרָע (chabburot petsa' tamriq bera')

a: Like water in irrigation ditches
p: Farmers steered water through small ditches with a foot or a hoe. God steers the king's heart as easily.
b: Palge mayim are irrigation channels, the network of ditches used in Egypt and Mesopotamia and in Israel's gardens (Deuteronomy 11:10 contrasts Egypt, watered "with your foot", with rain-fed Canaan). A gardener could turn the flow wherever he wanted. The most powerful man in the land is as easily directed by God. The Bible gives examples: Pharaoh's hardened heart (Exodus 9:12), Cyrus stirred to free the exiles (Ezra 1:1), Artaxerxes' favor to Ezra (Ezra 7:27). The Talmud cites the verse to show that a good king is a gift to pray for (Berakhot 55a).
orig: פַּלְגֵי־מַיִם לֶב־מֶלֶךְ בְּיַד־יְהוָה (palge-mayim lev-melekh beyad-YHWH)
r: 16:1; 16:9; Deuteronomy 11:10; Exodus 9:12; Ezra 1:1; Ezra 7:27; Isaiah 45:1–4; Daniel 4:31–32

a: but the LORD is the one who weighs hearts
p: Close to 16:2, with 'hearts' for 'spirits'. Each thinks himself right; God weighs the heart.
b: 16:2 has "weighs spirits" (ruchot), this verse "weighs hearts" (libbot); 24:12 asks whether the one who weighs hearts does not know. The Egyptian picture of the heart weighed on a balance at judgment lies behind the image (see 16:2). The first line repeats 12:15 and 16:2a in substance. Paul says that even a clear conscience does not make him righteous; the one who judges him is the Lord (1 Corinthians 4:4).

a: is something the LORD would choose over sacrifice
p: One of the few places in Proverbs that speaks of worship. Like the prophets, it ranks justice above offerings.
b: Proverbs seldom mentions the temple, and when it does it is in this prophetic key (15:8; 21:27). Samuel: "listening is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22). Hosea: "Loyal love is what I want, not sacrifice" (Hosea 6:6), which Jesus quotes twice (Matthew 9:13; Matthew 12:7). Amos 5:21–24 and Micah 6:6–8 say the same. None of these do away with sacrifice; they say God will not accept worship from people who ignore justice. The Greek renders: "to do righteous things and speak truth is more pleasing to God than the blood of sacrifices".
orig: עֲשֹׂה צְדָקָה וּמִשְׁפָּט נִבְחָר לַיהוָה מִזָּבַח ('asoh tsedaqah umishpat nivchar laYHWH mizzavach)
r: 15:8; 21:27; 1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21–24; Micah 6:6–8; Matthew 9:13; Matthew 12:7

a: the lamp of the wicked is sin
p: The word nir can mean 'lamp' or 'newly plowed ground'. Either way, all the wicked produce is sin.
b: The consonants of nir can be read as "lamp" (ner), the reading of the Greek, the Vulgate and the Targum, or as "fallow ground, tillage" (nir, Jeremiah 4:3; Hosea 10:12), which Rashi takes: the "plowing" of the wicked, their schemes, is sin. On the first reading, the wicked man's lamp, his life and success (13:9; 20:20), is itself sin. On the second, all his labor yields only sin. The first line, "lofty eyes", recalls the first of the seven things the LORD hates (6:17).
orig: נִר רְשָׁעִים חַטָּאת (nir resha'im chatta't)

a: everyone in a rush heads only to need
p: Diligence brings gain; haste brings want. The Greek lacks this verse.
b: The "diligent" (charuts, "sharp") man's plans come to profit (motar), as in 14:23. The one who is "hasty" ('ats, the word of 19:2) comes only to lack. Proverbs is not against speed in work (22:29) but against shortcuts, get-rich-quick schemes and impulsive decisions (13:11; 20:21; 28:20, 22). The saying is missing from the Greek.

a: those who seek it are seeking death
p: The Hebrew says those who seek such treasure seek death. The Greek and Vulgate have 'snares of death'.
b: Hevel niddaf is a "breath driven away", the vapor or vanity of Ecclesiastes (Ecclesiastes 1:2). The second line in the Hebrew is "seekers of death" (mevaqshe-mavet). Many scholars, following the Greek ("pursues vanity into snares of death") and the Vulgate ("will run into the snares of death"), read moqshe-mavet, "snares of death", as in 13:14 and 14:27. The difference is one letter. The Plain keeps the Hebrew; see the variant.
orig: הֶבֶל נִדָּף מְבַקְשֵׁי־מָוֶת (hevel niddaf mevaqshe-mavet)

a: A guilty man's road twists and turns
p: The words vazar ('guilty'?) and hafakhfakh ('twisting') appear only here. The sense is clear despite the rare words.
b: Hafakhfakh, "very crooked", doubles the root for turning over. Vazar appears nowhere else; most now link it to an Arabic word for "guilty" ("the way of a guilty man"). Older readers split it as ve-zar, "and strange", which the Vulgate ("the perverse way of a man is strange"), the Targum and Rashi ("a man who is strange, turning away from the commandment") follow. Either way the guilty man's path twists, and the pure man's conduct is straight.
orig: הֲפַכְפַּךְ דֶּרֶךְ אִישׁ וָזָר (hafakhpakh derekh ish vazar)

a: Living in a corner up on the roof is better
p: Flat roofs were living space; a small shelter or corner up there would be cramped and exposed. Repeated in 25:24.
b: Israelite houses had flat roofs reached by a ladder or stair, used for drying flax (Joshua 2:6), sleeping in hot weather (1 Samuel 9:25–26) and sometimes a small room (2 Kings 4:10). A "corner of the roof" (pinnat-gag), open to sun and rain, is a picture of the least comfort. It is better than sharing a house (bet chaver, a house in common) with a quarrelsome wife. 25:24 repeats the saying word for word, and 21:19 says the same with the desert. On the quarrelsome-wife sayings, see 19:13.
orig: טוֹב לָשֶׁבֶת עַל־פִּנַּת־גָּג (tov lashevet 'al-pinnat-gag)

a: When a mocker pays the fine, the naive grow wise
p: A second form of 19:25. The naive learn by watching the mocker punished; the wise learn by instruction.
b: In 19:25 the mocker is struck; here he "pays the fine" (ba'onesh, the word of 17:26 and 19:19). The second line differs: here "when the wise is instructed" (behaskil), there "when the discerning is reproved". The pairing of the mocker, the naive and the wise is the core of the book's purpose statement (1:4–5, 22).

a: The righteous one studies the house of the wicked
p: Is the 'righteous one' God, judging the wicked, or a righteous person who learns from watching their fall?
b: Line one says "a righteous one considers the house of the wicked"; line two "he overturns the wicked into ruin". If the subject of both lines is the same, the one who overthrows is God, called tsaddiq as in Job 34:17 and Deuteronomy 32:4. Rashi reads it so: "the Righteous One of the world". Others, with the Greek ("a righteous man understands the hearts of the ungodly"), the Vulgate and the Targum, take the righteous one as a human observer who learns from what happens to the wicked, while God (unnamed) overthrows them. The Plain keeps "the righteous one" lowercase and leaves the question open.
orig: מַשְׂכִּיל צַדִּיק לְבֵית רָשָׁע (maskil tsaddiq levet rasha')

a: Plug your ears to a poor man's cry
p: Whoever will not hear the poor will not be heard. Jesus' parable of the rich man and Lazarus turns on the same idea.
b: This is the measure-for-measure principle: the one who shuts his ears to the dal will cry and get no answer, from people or from God. The Law warns that the poor man's cry against an oppressor will be heard by God (Exodus 22:22–27; Deuteronomy 15:7–11; Deuteronomy 24:14–15). James: judgment has no mercy for the one who has shown none (James 2:13). Jesus' rich man ignores Lazarus at his gate and later begs in vain (Luke 16:19–31). In the Talmud, Rav Yehuda quotes it to his teacher Shmuel when Shmuel ignores a woman crying out about an injustice (Shabbat 55a).

a: a bribe tucked in the robe
p: This describes what works: a quiet gift calms anger. It does not approve bribing judges, which 17:23 condemns.
b: A "gift in secret" (mattan basseter) and a "bribe in the bosom" (shochad bacheq, the fold of the robe used as a pocket, as in 17:23) calm anger. Like 17:8 and 18:16, the saying observes how the world works. Some take it in a good sense, like Jacob's gift that appeased Esau (Genesis 32:20) or Abigail's to David (1 Samuel 25:18–35). But when such a gift goes to a judge it perverts justice, which the Law and Proverbs condemn (Exodus 23:8; 17:23). The Talmud reads "a gift in secret" as charity given in secret, which turns aside God's anger (Bava Batra 9b).
orig: מַתָּן בַּסֵּתֶר יִכְפֶּה־אָף (mattan basseter yikhpeh-af)

a: will end up resting with the assembly of the shades
p: The Rephaim are the shades of the dead in Sheol. In other texts the same name is used of an ancient race of giants.
b: Refa'im in poetry are the dead, shadowy figures in Sheol who "rise" to greet the fallen king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:9) and do not praise God (Psalm 88:10). Proverbs has the strange woman's guests among them (2:18; 9:18). In Ugaritic texts the rpum are the royal dead, honored ancestors. The Bible also uses the name of an old race of giants in Canaan (Deuteronomy 2:11, 20; Deuteronomy 3:11), which is why the Greek and the Vulgate say "the assembly of giants" here. Rashi: "the congregation of Gehinnom". The man who strays from good sense will "rest" there for good.
orig: בִּקְהַל רְפָאִים יָנוּחַ (biqhal refa'im yanuach)
r: 2:18; 9:18; Isaiah 14:9; Isaiah 26:14; Isaiah 26:19; Psalm 88:10; Job 26:5; Deuteronomy 2:11

a: love wine and oil and you will not grow rich
p: Wine and scented oil were the luxuries of a feast. Someone who lives for parties will not build up wealth.
b: Simchah, "pleasure" or merriment, here means feasting. Wine and perfumed oil for anointing the head were the marks of a banquet (Psalm 23:5; Amos 6:6; Ecclesiastes 9:7–8). Proverbs does not condemn them: 21:20 says the wise man's house has stores of oil. The saying is about loving them, a life spent on parties. Amos denounces the rich of Samaria who drink wine from bowls and anoint themselves with the finest oils but do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph (Amos 6:4–6).
orig: אֹהֵב יַיִן־וָשֶׁמֶן לֹא יַעֲשִׁיר (ohev yayin-vashemen lo ya'ashir)

a: The wicked man is the price paid to ransom the righteous
p: The wicked take the place of the righteous in disaster. Rashi gives Haman taking Mordecai's place on the gallows.
b: Kofer is a ransom price, the payment that buys a life (Exodus 21:30; Exodus 30:12). The saying does not mean that the wicked atone for the righteous. It means that the disaster the wicked planned or deserved falls on them while the righteous go free, as in 11:8: "The righteous man gets pulled free of trouble, / and the wicked man takes his place in it". Rashi gives Mordecai and Haman (Esther 7:10). Isaiah 43:3 uses kofer of nations given as Israel's ransom.
orig: כֹּפֶר לַצַּדִּיק רָשָׁע (kofer latstsaddiq rasha')

a: but a fool of a man swallows it up
p: The wise man has stores laid by; the fool consumes everything as it comes.
b: "Treasure to be desired and oil" in the wise man's dwelling (naveh) are the provisions of a prudent household, like the ant's stores (6:8) and Joseph's granaries (Genesis 41:35–36). The "fool of a man" (kesil adam) "swallows it" (yevall'ennu), spending what he has as soon as he gets it. The Greek reads the first line of the wise man's mouth: "a desirable treasure will rest on the mouth of the wise". Jesus' rich fool, by contrast, stored up for himself and was not rich toward God (Luke 12:16–21).

a: One wise man can climb into a city full of warriors
p: A wise man can take a city the strong defend. Ecclesiastes tells a story on the theme.
b: Wisdom is greater than military might (24:5–6). Ecclesiastes 9:13–16 tells of a small city besieged by a great king and saved by a poor wise man, whom nobody remembered afterward, and concludes that wisdom is better than strength. David's men took Jerusalem by a strategy through the water shaft (2 Samuel 5:6–8), and the wise woman of Abel saved her city by negotiation (2 Samuel 20:16–22). Paul uses the image of tearing down strongholds of argument (2 Corinthians 10:4–5).

a: The proud, puffed-up man has a name: Mocker
p: A definition: the mocker is the arrogant man whose pride overflows. The verse lines up three words for pride.
b: Zed (proud), yahir (haughty) and 'evrat zadon (an overflow of insolence) define the lets. The mocker of Proverbs is not just a joker but someone too proud to be taught (9:7–8; 13:1; 15:12). Rashi: the haughty man will end up a scorner, "for he does not care to hear reproof". The happy person of Psalm 1:1 "does not sit where mockers sit".
orig: זֵד יָהִיר לֵץ שְׁמוֹ (zed yahir lets shemo)

a: What a lazy person craves is what kills him
p: The lazy one wants things but won't work for them, and that unmet craving destroys him.
b: The lazy one's "desire" (ta'avah) kills him because it is never joined to effort; compare 13:4, "The lazy one craves, but his appetite gets nothing". 21:26 continues the thought: he craves all day, while the righteous man gives without holding back. The contrast is not between the rich and the poor but between grasping and giving. Paul: "if anyone is unwilling to work, he should not eat either" (2 Thessalonians 3:10); and he tells the former thief to work with his hands so that he has something to give to anyone in need (Ephesians 4:28).

a: still worse if they bring it with a scheme in mind
p: The wicked man's sacrifice is abhorrent already; worse when he offers it to gain something by it.
b: The first line repeats 15:8a. The second adds that it is worse when it is brought bezimmah, "with a scheme" (zimmah, a plan, usually evil), as if to bribe God or to cover a crime with a show of piety. Absalom asked leave to go and pay a vow in Hebron in order to launch his revolt (2 Samuel 15:7–12), and Jezebel proclaimed a fast to frame Naboth (1 Kings 21:9–13). The Greek: "for they offer them lawlessly". Rabbi Yochanan cites the first line in a ruling on offerings from a condemned town (Sanhedrin 112b).
orig: אַף כִּי־בְזִמָּה יְבִיאֶנּוּ (af ki-vezimmah yevi'ennu)

a: but someone who listens will have the last word
p: The lying witness will perish, but the one who listens carefully will speak 'to the end', with lasting effect.
b: Lanetsach, "forever" or "to victory", is unclear. It may mean the careful listener's testimony will stand, or that he will speak on and on while the false witness is silenced, or that he will "speak successfully". The Vulgate has "an obedient man speaks victory". Rashi takes "one who listens" as obeying the Torah's ban on false witness. The point is that a witness who listens before he speaks gives testimony that lasts.
orig: וְאִישׁ שׁוֹמֵעַ לָנֶצַח יְדַבֵּר (ve'ish shomea' lanetsach yedabber)

a: but the upright man thinks through his way
p: The written text says the upright man 'establishes' his way, the reading tradition that he 'considers' it.
b: The wicked man "makes his face hard" (he'ez befanav), a brazen look, as the adulteress does in 7:13. The upright man, by contrast, thinks about where he is going, the habit of the shrewd in 14:8 and 14:15. The written and read forms of the verb differ by one stroke, "establishes" or "considers"; see the variant.
orig: וְיָשָׁר הוּא יָבִין דַּרְכּוֹ (veyashar hu yavin darko) Qere; Ketiv יָכִין דְּרָכָיו (yakhin derakhav)

a: There is no wisdom, no understanding
p: No human wisdom or plan can stand against God, however wise it looks.
b: The threefold "there is no" (en) puts all human cleverness under God. Wisdom, understanding and counsel are the book's own ideals, and none of them can succeed "in front of" or "against" the LORD (leneged YHWH). Ahithophel's counsel was "like a word of God", yet God defeated it (2 Samuel 16:23; 2 Samuel 17:14). Paul quotes Job and Isaiah to say that God catches the wise in their craftiness (1 Corinthians 1:19; 1 Corinthians 3:19). The Talmud reads it to mean that where God's name is profaned, one need not first defer to a teacher, and so explains why Phinehas acted at once (Numbers 25:7; Sanhedrin 82a).

a: You may get the horse ready for the day of war
p: Horses were the tanks of the ancient world, and Israel's kings were warned against relying on them.
b: War horses pulled chariots and later carried cavalry, the strongest force of Egypt and Assyria. The Law told Israel's king not to multiply horses (Deuteronomy 17:16), Solomon did so anyway (1 Kings 10:26–29), and the Psalms and prophets warn against trusting them: "These have chariots, and those have horses, / but we call on the name of the LORD our God" (Psalm 20:7; compare Psalm 33:16–17; Isaiah 31:1). The proverb does not say not to prepare; it says victory (teshu'ah, rescue) belongs to the LORD.
orig: סוּס מוּכָן לְיוֹם מִלְחָמָה (sus mukhan leyom milchamah)
r: Deuteronomy 17:16; 1 Kings 10:26–29; Psalm 20:7; Psalm 33:16–17; Isaiah 31:1; 1 Samuel 17:47

a: A name is worth choosing over great riches
p: A person's reputation is worth more than wealth. Ecclesiastes says a good name is better than fine perfume.
b: Shem, "name", means reputation, standing in the community, and the memory a person leaves (10:7). "Favor" (chen), being well thought of, is better than silver and gold. Ecclesiastes 7:1 plays on the sounds: tov shem mishshemen tov, "better a good name than good oil". The Greek adds "good" to the name, "a good name is more to be chosen". Proverbs often ranks wisdom and character above wealth (3:14–15; 8:10–11; 16:16).
orig: נִבְחָר שֵׁם מֵעֹשֶׁר רָב (nivchar shem me'osher rav)

a: the LORD made all of them
p: Rich and poor stand on the same ground, since one God made both. 29:13 says nearly the same.
b: "Meet" (nifgashu) may mean they live side by side, or that they share a common level before God. Either way, the LORD is the maker of both, so wealth gives no one higher standing with him. 29:13 is a twin: "the poor man and the oppressor meet; the LORD gives light to the eyes of both." Job grounds his care for his slaves in the same thought (Job 31:13–15), and Proverbs uses it to protect the poor (14:31; 17:5). James rebukes a church that seats the rich in honor and the poor on the floor (James 2:1–7).
orig: עָשִׁיר וָרָשׁ נִפְגָּשׁוּ (ashir varash nifgashu)

a: A shrewd person sees trouble coming and takes cover
p: Repeated almost word for word in 27:12. Shrewdness here is simple foresight.
b: 27:12 repeats the saying with small changes. The 'arum, the "shrewd", is the positive side of a word that can also mean crafty (the serpent of Genesis 3:1). Here it is plain foresight: seeing danger ahead and getting out of the way. The naive (peta'im) walk straight on and "pay for it" (ne'enashu, are fined). Jesus tells his disciples to be "be sharp like snakes and pure like doves" (Matthew 10:16). The Greek expands: the shrewd one, seeing a wicked man punished, is himself strongly instructed.
orig: עָרוּם רָאָה רָעָה וְנִסְתָּר ('arum ra'ah ra'ah venistar)

a: Humility, the fear of the LORD, brings its payoff
p: Literally 'the heel (result) of humility is the fear of the LORD'. The two may be one thing, or one may lead to the other.
b: 'Eqev is "heel", then "consequence, reward" (Psalm 19:11). The Hebrew puts "humility" and "the fear of the LORD" side by side without a joining word. The Plain takes them as one thing named twice (compare 15:33, where the fear of the LORD is discipline and humility comes before honor). Others read "the reward of humility is the fear of the LORD", and Rashi gives both: humility brings fear of the LORD, or humility is the main virtue and fear is its heel. Riches, honor and life are what wisdom offers in 3:16 and 8:18.
orig: עֵקֶב עֲנָוָה יִרְאַת יְהוָה ('eqev 'anavah yir'at YHWH)

a: Train a young person according to his way
p: Chanakh means to dedicate or start, and gives Hanukkah its name. Na'ar covers anyone from a baby to a young man.
b: Chanokh elsewhere means to dedicate a new house (Deuteronomy 20:5) or the temple (1 Kings 8:63), and the noun chanukkah is a dedication (Numbers 7:84; Psalm 30 title). Here it means to start a young person off, to set him in a way. An old explanation links it to rubbing a newborn's palate with date paste to start him feeding, but this is a guess. Na'ar can be a baby (Exodus 2:6), a boy (1 Samuel 1:24), a young man of seventeen (Genesis 37:2), or a servant or squire (Genesis 22:3; 1 Samuel 14:1). Ted Hildebrandt argued that here it means a young man of status being trained for his role; the Talmud's rabbis set ages 16–22 or 18–24 for this training (Kiddushin 30a).
orig: חֲנֹךְ לַנַּעַר עַל־פִּי דַרְכּוֹ (chanokh lanna'ar 'al-pi darko)
r: Deuteronomy 20:5; 1 Kings 8:63; Numbers 7:84; Exodus 2:6; Genesis 37:2; 1 Samuel 1:24; 1 Samuel 14:1

a: even after he grows old, he will not leave it
t: Which 'way'? And is it a promise?
p: 'His way' may be the right way, the child's own bent, or his own willful path. And it states a rule, not a guarantee.
b: "According to his way" ('al-pi darko, literally "on the mouth of his way") is read three ways. (1) The way he should go, the moral way of the book: the traditional reading, and the KJV's. (2) His own aptitude: train each child as he is made. Ralbag, Malbim and Metzudat David read it so, and Delitzsch argued for it. (3) Irony: let a boy have his own way and he will never leave it, a warning, as some modern commentators read it. Rashi's reading is neutral: what you teach a child, good or bad, he keeps. Like all proverbs, the saying states what usually happens, not a promise; the book itself knows of sons who reject their fathers (17:21, 25; 30:11). The Greek lacks the verse; the Vulgate opens it with "It is a proverb".
orig: גַּם כִּי־יַזְקִין לֹא־יָסוּר מִמֶּנָּה (gam ki-yazqin lo-yasur mimmennah)

a: the one who borrows becomes the lender's slave
p: In the ancient world, a man who could not repay a debt could be forced into slavery, or have his children taken.
b: This is not a figure of speech. A creditor could seize a debtor's children as slaves (2 Kings 4:1), and in Nehemiah's time families mortgaged fields and sold sons and daughters to pay debts (Nehemiah 5:1–5). The Law limited debt slavery to six years and canceled debts in the seventh year (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:1–18), and it forbade charging interest to a fellow Israelite (Leviticus 25:35–37). Deuteronomy promises that obedient Israel will lend and not borrow (Deuteronomy 15:6; 28:12). Rashi reads it of learning: the unlearned always needs the scholar. The Talmud sets it beside 19:17 (Bava Batra 10a).
orig: וְעֶבֶד לֹוֶה לְאִישׁ מַלְוֶה (ve'eved loveh le'ish malveh)
r: 19:17; 2 Kings 4:1; Nehemiah 5:1–5; Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:1–18; Leviticus 25:35–37; Romans 13:8

a: Plant wrongdoing and you will harvest disaster
p: The farming picture of reaping what you sow. Paul uses it, and the Greek adds a line Paul seems to echo.
b: Eliphaz uses the same image: "whoever plows wickedness and plants misery gets a harvest of it" (Job 4:8), and Hosea: "They sow wind, so a storm wind is what they will reap" (Hosea 8:7). The second line is harder: "the rod of his fury will fail", the power he used in anger will end. Rashi gives two readings, the second the same as the Plain's. Paul: "Whatever a person sows, that is what he will also reap" (Galatians 6:7). After this verse the Greek adds a couplet, "God blesses a cheerful man and a giver", which Paul seems to echo in "God loves a glad giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7); see the variant.
orig: זוֹרֵעַ עַוְלָה יִקְצָר־אָוֶן (zorea' 'avlah yiqtsar-aven)

a: The person with a kind eye will be blessed
p: Literally 'good of eye': generous. The 'evil eye' in Hebrew idiom is stinginess.
b: Tov-'ayin, "good of eye", is the generous person; the "evil eye" (ra' 'ayin) is the grudging, stingy one (23:6; 28:22; Deuteronomy 15:9). Jesus uses the idiom: "If your eye is sound, light will fill your whole body" (Matthew 6:22), and the landowner asks, "is your eye evil because I am good?" (Matthew 20:15). The good-eyed man is "blessed" because he gives his bread to the poor. The Greek adds a couplet: "He who gives gifts gains victory and honor, but he takes away the soul of those who possess them".
orig: טוֹב־עַיִן הוּא יְבֹרָךְ (tov-'ayin hu yevorakh)

a: Throw out the mocker and the fighting leaves with him
p: Some trouble has a single source. Remove the scoffer and the quarrels end.
b: The mocker (lets) is the one who will not be corrected (21:24), so there is no point in arguing with him; the only remedy is removal. Ishmael's mocking led Sarah to say "Throw out this slave woman and her son" (Genesis 21:10), and Paul quotes the verse (Galatians 4:30). Paul also tells Titus to have nothing more to do with a divisive man after two warnings (Titus 3:10). The Greek places the scene in a council: "Cast out a pest from the assembly, and strife will go out with him".

a: Whoever loves purity of heart, whose lips speak grace
p: The Hebrew is awkward but the sense is clear: a man of pure heart and gracious speech wins the king's friendship.
b: The line reads literally "one who loves purity of heart, grace of his lips, his friend is a king". Kings needed honest advisers who could speak well (16:13; 25:11–12), and "the king's friend" was an official title at Solomon's court (1 Kings 4:5). The Greek makes God the subject: "The Lord loves holy hearts, and all the blameless are acceptable to him; a king shepherds with his lips." Jesus says, "Blessed are those whose hearts are pure, because they will see God" (Matthew 5:8).
orig: אֹהֵב טְהָר־לֵב חֵן שְׂפָתָיו רֵעֵהוּ מֶלֶךְ (ohev tehar-lev chen sefatav re'ehu melekh)

a: I will be murdered in the middle of the town square!
p: The lazy one's excuse is absurd: a lion in the town. It is meant to make the reader laugh. 26:13 repeats it.
b: Lions lived in the thickets of the Jordan and the hills (Jeremiah 49:19; Judges 14:5), but not in town squares. The lazy one invents the danger to stay in bed, and adds a second, "I will be murdered", using ratsach, the verb of the commandment against murder. The comedy is the point: excuses for not working are often as unlikely as this. 26:13 has a doublet. Rashi: the lazy one's question is "How shall I go out to learn Torah?"
orig: אֲרִי בַחוּץ בְּתוֹךְ רְחֹבוֹת אֵרָצֵחַ (ari vachuts betokh rechovot eratseach)

a: The mouth of strange women is a deep pit
p: A brief return of the 'strange woman' of chapters 2–7, whose smooth speech traps young men.
b: Zarot, "strange women" (plural only here), are the women outside a man's marriage whom chapters 2, 5, 6 and 7 warn against; their smooth speech is the trap (2:16; 5:3; 7:21). A deep pit (shuchah 'amuqqah) was used for trapping animals, and 23:27 repeats the image for the prostitute. "The one the LORD is angry with" (ze'um YHWH) falls into it: the fall is itself a judgment. Rashi takes the woman as an idolatress. The Greek has "the mouth of a lawless man" and adds three lines about evil ways.
orig: שׁוּחָה עֲמֻקָּה פִּי זָרוֹת (shuchah 'amuqqah pi zarot)

a: a disciplining rod is what will put it far from him
p: Proverbs assumes that physical punishment of children was right. Readers today disagree about what that means for them.
b: Shevet is a stick or staff, the shepherd's rod, the scepter, and also a tribe. Proverbs speaks of the rod on children in 13:24; 22:15; 23:13–14 and 29:15, and on fools' backs in 10:13 and 26:3. The text plainly means beating with a stick, which was normal in the ancient world; Egyptian school texts speak just as openly of beating pupils. Its goal is the child's good: folly is "bound up" (qeshurah) in him and discipline loosens it. The limit set in 19:18 and Ephesians 6:4 belongs beside it. How Jewish and Christian teachers apply these verses today, and where they disagree, is set out at 13:24 and on the chapter 13 page.
orig: שֵׁבֶט מוּסָר יַרְחִיקֶנָּה מִמֶּנּוּ (shevet musar yarchiqennah mimmennu)

a: give presents to the rich, and you will end up in want
p: A compressed verse. Both oppressing the poor and fawning on the rich lead in the end to want.
b: The Hebrew is "one who oppresses the poor to increase for him, one who gives to the rich, only to want". The Plain reads two subjects heading for the same end: the man who exploits the poor to get rich, and the man who gives gifts to the rich to buy favor, both come to poverty. Another reading takes "for him" as the poor man: oppressing the poor only increases him (God takes his side), while giving to the rich only produces want. Rashi: such a man will end by giving his money to rich foreign kings. The verse closes the first Solomon collection.
orig: עֹשֵׁק דָּל לְהַרְבּוֹת לוֹ נֹתֵן לְעָשִׁיר אַךְ־לְמַחְסוֹר ('osheq dal leharbot lo noten le'ashir akh-lemachsor)

a: Lean in and listen to the words of the wise
p: A new section begins here, running to 24:22. Its opening closely follows the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope.
b: After 375 one-verse sayings, the style changes: the teacher speaks in the first person, and the sayings become longer warnings in "do not" form. "The words of the wise" may be the heading of the collection, worked into the first line; 24:23 begins an appendix, "These also are of the wise". E. A. Wallis Budge, who published the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope in 1923, noted its likeness to Hebrew wisdom, and in 1924 Adolf Erman showed in detail that 22:17–23:11 runs parallel to it. Amenemope's first chapter begins "I pray thee to lend me thine ears, hearken to the things that will be said" (Budge's translation), and goes on: "deposit them in the treasure-house of thy belly" and "they will form a guiding support in thy tongue" (compare 22:17–18). See the chapter page.
orig: הַט אָזְנְךָ וּשְׁמַע דִּבְרֵי חֲכָמִים (hat oznekha ushema' divre chakhamim)

a: It is a pleasant thing to store them in your belly
p: The belly was the seat of memory and inner life. The sayings are to be stored inside and ready on the lips.
b: Beten, the belly, is the inner self (18:8; 20:27). Words stored there are memorized and ready to say, "set in place together on your lips" (yikkonu yachdav). Amenemope uses the same pair: "deposit them in the treasure-house of thy belly", and "they will form a guiding support in thy tongue". Egyptian scribes learned their instructions by copying and reciting them. Rashi: they will be kept in your heart when they are established on your lips, that is, when you say them aloud.
orig: כִּי־נָעִים כִּי־תִשְׁמְרֵם בְּבִטְנֶךָ (ki-na'im ki-tishmerem bevitnekha)

a: so that the LORD will be the one you trust
p: This line has no parallel in Amenemope. It states the aim of the whole collection in Israel's terms.
b: Whatever the Hebrew sage took from Egypt, he set it under a new purpose: "so that your trust may be in the LORD" (lihyot baYHWH mivtachekha). The phrase echoes 3:5, "Trust the LORD with your whole heart", and Jeremiah 17:7. Amenemope has his own piety, and speaks of "the god", but the name YHWH and the aim of trust in him are the Hebrew collection's own. The repeated "you, yes you" (af-attah) makes the teaching personal.
orig: לִהְיוֹת בַּיהוָה מִבְטַחֶךָ (lihyot baYHWH mivtachekha)

a: Haven't I put thirty sayings in writing for you
p: The Hebrew word here is unclear. Since 1924 most scholars read 'thirty', matching Amenemope's 'thirty chapters'.
b: The written text has shilshom, "day before yesterday", which elsewhere always comes with "yesterday" and means "formerly". The reading tradition has shalishim, "officers" or, as the KJV took it, "excellent things". Ancient translations read a form of "three": the Greek trissōs, "three times", the Vulgate tripliciter, the Targum "three times". Rashi reads "thirds": Torah, Prophets and Writings. Amenemope's last chapter begins: "Behold the Thirty Chapters! They will give [thee] pleasure, they will teach [thee]". With the same consonants a Hebrew reader can read sheloshim, "thirty", and most modern scholars and translations do. The Plain follows that reading. See the variant.
orig: הֲלֹא כָתַבְתִּי לְךָ שָׁלִשִׁים (halo khatavti lekha shalishim); Ketiv שִׁלְשׁוֹם (shilshom)

a: so you can carry back a true answer to the ones who sent you
p: The pupil is trained as an official who carries messages and reports back. Amenemope's prologue says the same.
b: The setting is a court or office, where young men were trained to serve as messengers and officials. Amenemope's prologue says the teaching will enable a man "to know how to return a suitable answer to him that has spoken to him, [and] to carry back a [satisfactory] report to the man who has despatched him on a mission". The Hebrew stresses truth: qosht imre emet, "the certainty of true words". An envoy you can trust "is like a chill of snow in harvest time" (25:13); a bad one is like cutting off one's own feet (26:6). Rashi takes the senders as those who ask you for instruction.
orig: לְהָשִׁיב אֲמָרִים אֱמֶת לְשֹׁלְחֶיךָ (lehashiv amarim emet leshole'chekha)

a: Do not rob a poor man just because he is poor
p: Amenemope's second chapter opens: 'Guard thyself against plundering the poor man'. The Hebrew adds the LORD.
b: The Plain takes "because he is poor" as the robber's reason: he is easy to rob. The "gate" was the court, where elders sat to judge (Ruth 4:1–11; Amos 5:12, 15). Amenemope chapter 2: "Guard thyself against plundering the poor man and from treating with harshness the destitute." The Hebrew's next line gives the reason: the LORD will take the case (22:23). The Talmud cites 22:22–23 against a judge who takes money from one side and gives it to the other unjustly: God takes that judge's life (Sanhedrin 7a).
orig: אַל־תִּגְזָל־דָּל כִּי דַל־הוּא (al-tigzol-dal ki dal-hu)

a: he will rob of life those who rob them
p: God acts as the poor man's lawyer in court and turns the robber's verb back on him.
b: Yariv rivam, "he will plead their case", is the language of a lawsuit (23:11; Psalm 43:1; Micah 7:9). The rare verb qava', "rob", is used twice: the LORD will rob the robbers of their life. Malachi uses it of Israel robbing God of tithes (Malachi 3:8–9). Rashi explains the word from Aramaic, where it means robbery. The God who defends the widow and orphan (Exodus 22:22–24; Psalm 68:5) defends the poor in court when no human advocate will.
orig: כִּי־יְהוָה יָרִיב רִיבָם וְקָבַע אֶת־קֹבְעֵיהֶם נָפֶשׁ (ki-YHWH yariv rivam veqava' et-qov'ehem nafesh)

a: Do not keep company with a man ruled by anger
p: Amenemope says nearly the same: 'Make not to be a friend of thine the hasty, hot-headed man.' Bad tempers are catching.
b: "A man ruled by anger" is literally "a master of anger" (ba'al af), and "someone full of rage" is "a man of heat" (ish chemot). Amenemope's ninth chapter: "Make not to be a friend of thine the hasty, hot-headed man". Amenemope contrasts the "heated man" with the truly silent man throughout, the same pair as 17:27. 22:25 gives the reason: you learn his ways. Compare 13:20, "The one who walks with the wise grows wise", and the proverb Paul quotes, that bad company wrecks good habits (1 Corinthians 15:33).
orig: אַל־תִּתְרַע אֶת־בַּעַל אָף (al-titra' et-ba'al af)

a: and set a trap for your own life
p: Character rubs off. Spend time with an angry man and you take on his ways, which become a snare.
b: Te'elaf, "you learn", is the root of aluf, a close companion (16:28). Ways learned by habit become a snare (moqesh) for the learner. The Greek: "lest you learn his ways and take snares for your soul". The same idea of picking up others' habits underlies the warnings against bad company in 1:10–19 and 13:20.

a: Do not join those who clap hands on a pledge
p: Amenemope has no saying on surety. This is one of the Hebrew collection's own warnings.
b: "Clapping hands" (toq'e-khaf) sealed an agreement to stand good for someone else's debt (6:1; 17:18). Proverbs warns against it repeatedly (6:1–5; 11:15; 17:18; 20:16; 27:13). Amenemope has no parallel to 22:26–27, which shows that the Hebrew collection was not a translation: the sage mixed Egyptian material with Israel's own. The Targum reads it as "for your neighbor".
orig: אַל־תְּהִי בְתֹקְעֵי־כָף (al-tehi veToq'e-khaf)

a: why let them take the bed right out from under you?
p: Creditors could take anything, even the bed a man slept on. The Talmud read 'bed' as a man's wife.
b: When the surety cannot pay, the creditor seizes his property, down to his bed (mishkav). The Law protected a poor man's cloak overnight (Exodus 22:26–27), but a guarantor who had vouched for someone else's debt could lose even the bed under him. The Talmud reads "bed" as a man's wife: in one teaching his wife dies because of unpaid vows (Shabbat 32b), in another because of debts he cannot pay (Sanhedrin 22a). The Vulgate has "the covering from your bed".
orig: לָמָּה יִקַּח מִשְׁכָּבְךָ מִתַּחְתֶּיךָ (lammah yiqqach mishkavekha mittachtekha)

a: Do not shift the old boundary line
p: Moving a boundary stone stole a family's inheritance. The Law, Amenemope and this saying all forbid it.
b: Fields were marked with stones or posts, and a neighbor could move one at night to steal a strip of land. The Law curses whoever moves his neighbor's boundary marker (Deuteronomy 19:14; Deuteronomy 27:17), and the prophets condemn it (Hosea 5:10; compare Job 24:2). In Israel land was the family's share in the LORD's gift (Leviticus 25:23; 1 Kings 21:3). Amenemope's sixth chapter warns against robbing land "when thou art assessing the bounds of the estate of the widow" and says "Take good heed concerning the treading down of the boundaries of the fields" (Budge; later translators read its first line as moving a field's boundary stone, where Budge saw a tomb marker). Proverbs 23:10 repeats this saying and adds "the fields of orphans". The Greek has "eternal boundaries".
orig: אַל־תַּסֵּג גְּבוּל עוֹלָם (al-tasseg gevul 'olam)
r: 23:10–11; Deuteronomy 19:14; Deuteronomy 27:17; Hosea 5:10; Job 24:2; Leviticus 25:23; 1 Kings 21:3

a: You see a man who is quick at his work?
p: Mahir means quick, skilled, expert, as of Ezra the expert scribe. Amenemope ends with the skilled scribe at court.
b: Mahir describes Ezra, rendered on this site "an expert in Moses' law" (Ezra 7:6), and the psalmist's tongue, "the pen of a swift scribe" (Psalm 45:1). The skilled worker will "take his stand" (yityatsev) before kings, serving at court, not before "obscure people" (chashukkim, "dark ones"). Joseph and Daniel rose this way (Genesis 41:39–46; Daniel 1:19–20). Amenemope's last chapter ends: a scribe "who would make himself to be pre-eminent in his profession" will "find himself to be of equal importance with the Smeru (i.e., the 'friends' of the King)". The Talmud has a heavenly voice quote the verse in praise of Solomon, who finished God's house before his own (Sanhedrin 104b).
orig: חָזִיתָ אִישׁ מָהִיר בִּמְלַאכְתּוֹ (chazita ish mahir bimla'khto)
r: Ezra 7:6; Psalm 45:1; Genesis 41:39–46; Daniel 1:19–20; 1 Kings 11:28; Ecclesiastes 9:10
